Q1L1NAT / ROUTING
SCENARIO

A private EC2 instance has no public IPv4 address and cannot reach package repositories on the internet. Walk me through the exact AWS path the packet should take and the first checks you would make.

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A private EC2 instance has no public IPv4 address and cannot reach package repositories on the internet. Walk me through the exact AWS path the packet should take and the first checks you would make
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNETWORKING
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
For production Multi-AZ egress, same-AZ NAT routing avoids cross-AZ dependency and data transfer; VPC endpoints can remove AWS-service traffic from NAT.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private workload → Private route table → same-AZ NAT Gateway → Public route table → Internet Gateway → Internet
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT-A
  • VPC CIDR → local
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
  • NAT Gateway has EIP
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

The application belongs in a private subnet with no public IPv4 address. Its private route table should send 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT Gateway in the same AZ. The NAT Gateway must be in a public subnet with an Elastic IP, and that public subnet needs 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway. Security Groups remain stateful and NACLs must allow the required return traffic. This gives outbound IPv4 internet access without making the workload directly reachable from the internet.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_eip, aws_nat_gateway, aws_route_table, aws_route, aws_route_table_association, aws_internet_gateway, aws_subnet

Resource relationships

Each private subnet is explicitly associated with a private route table. Its IPv4 default route targets the NAT Gateway in the same AZ. Each NAT Gateway is created in a public subnet with an EIP; the public route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the VPC Internet Gateway.

Production pattern

Create one NAT per active AZ for production HA. Drive subnets/NAT/routes from a single AZ map so a private subnet cannot accidentally point to another AZ. Keep NAT and route-table ownership in the network stack, not application stacks.

Representative Terraform
locals {
  azs = {
    a = { public = aws_subnet.public_a.id, private = aws_subnet.private_a.id }
    b = { public = aws_subnet.public_b.id, private = aws_subnet.private_b.id }
  }
}
resource "aws_eip" "nat" {
  for_each = local.azs
  domain   = "vpc"
}
resource "aws_nat_gateway" "az" {
  for_each      = local.azs
  subnet_id     = each.value.public
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat[each.key].id
}
resource "aws_route" "private_default" {
  for_each               = local.azs
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private[each.key].id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.az[each.key].id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "private" {
  for_each       = local.azs
  subnet_id      = each.value.private
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private[each.key].id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Plan must show same-AZ NAT targets and no route-table replacement. Verify with route-table associations, NAT metrics and an HTTPS egress test from every AZ. Add alarms for NAT errors/port pressure and tag all per-AZ resources consistently.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. Wrong private-subnet route-table association
  2. 0.0.0.0/0 points to wrong NAT
  3. NAT in wrong/public route missing IGW
  4. NACL/DNS issue
  5. Cross-AZ NAT dependency or cost
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Private workloads stay non-addressable from the internet while retaining outbound IPv4 access. Per-AZ NAT removes a single-AZ dependency and cross-AZ egress, at the cost of more NAT Gateway hourly charges.
Q2L1PUBLIC SUBNET
SCENARIO

An EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address, but users on the internet cannot reach TCP 443. What has to be true for that instance to actually be internet-reachable, and how would you troubleshoot it?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
An EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address, but users on the internet cannot reach TCP 443. What has to be true for that instance to actually be internet-reachable, and how would you troubleshoot it
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNETWORKING
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Public reachability requires the complete chain: public IP + subnet route to IGW + security controls + application listener.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Internet → Internet Gateway → Public subnet route table → EC2 public IPv4/ENI → Security Group/NACL → Application
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
  • 10.0.0.0/16 → local
  • Public IPv4/EIP present
  • SG inbound + NACL path allowed
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

A public IPv4 address alone does not make an EC2 instance reachable. I would verify that the subnet is actually public by checking its route table for 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, confirm the IGW is attached, and verify the instance has the expected public IPv4/EIP on its ENI. Then I would check the Security Group inbound rule for the application port, the subnet NACL in both directions and whether the OS/application is listening on that port. NAT Gateway is not part of inbound reachability to a public instance.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc, aws_subnet, aws_internet_gateway, aws_route_table, aws_route, aws_route_table_association, aws_instance/launch_template, aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule

Resource relationships

The public subnet route table targets the attached IGW for 0.0.0.0/0. The instance or ENI needs public addressing, the Security Group permits TCP 443 from the approved source, and the application must actually listen on 443. NACLs must permit the flow if customized.

Production pattern

Prefer an internet-facing ALB in public subnets with application instances private. If direct EC2 exposure is required, make the public-addressing and route-table association explicit rather than relying on console defaults.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "this" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.this.id }
resource "aws_route" "public_default" {
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.public.id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  gateway_id             = aws_internet_gateway.this.id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "public" {
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.public_a.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "https" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.web.id
  cidr_ipv4         = var.allowed_client_cidr
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port = 443
  to_port   = 443
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Do not use 0.0.0.0/0 on administrative ports. Validate public-IP assignment/EIP separately from routing. In production, prefer ALB + private targets + SSM Session Manager instead of inbound SSH.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. No IGW default route
  2. No public IPv4/EIP
  3. SG inbound missing
  4. NACL return rule missing
  5. Application not listening
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

A public IPv4 address is only one requirement. Internet reachability needs the subnet's associated route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 to an attached Internet Gateway, and the instance still needs SG/NACL rules plus a listening application. This separation helps isolate whether the failure is routing, security, or the host itself.

Q3L1LOCAL ROUTING
SCENARIO

EC2-A in a private subnet in AZ-A cannot connect to EC2-B in a private subnet in AZ-B on TCP 8080. Both are in the same VPC. Walk me through the path and isolate the likely failure domains.

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
EC2-A in a private subnet in AZ-A cannot connect to EC2-B in a private subnet in AZ-B on TCP 8080. Both are in the same VPC. Walk me through the path and isolate the likely failure domains
SCOPE
Multi-AZAZ-AAZ-BSame VPCPrivate subnet
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Same-VPC east-west traffic uses the immutable local route; NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway are not in this packet path.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
EC2-A 10.0.11.10 ↓ TCP 8080 Source SG egress ↓ Subnet-A NACL ↓ VPC local route: 10.0.0.0/16 → local ↓ Subnet-B NACL ↓ Destination SG ingress: TCP 8080 from client-sg ↓ EC2-B 10.0.12.20:8080 ↓ Application process / OS firewall Key point: Both instances are in the same VPC, so this traffic uses the VPC local route. NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway are not involved.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • client-sg: egress TCP 8080
  • app-sg: ingress TCP 8080 from client-sg
  • Allow request direction
  • Allow ephemeral return traffic
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Because both EC2 instances are in the same VPC, I would first rule out the NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway because neither is part of this traffic path.

I would confirm the source and destination private IP addresses and verify that the VPC route table still has the local route for 10.0.0.0/16. Traffic between 10.0.11.10 in AZ-A and 10.0.12.20 in AZ-B should stay on the AWS VPC network.

Next I would check the destination security group on EC2-B. For an application listening on TCP 8080, I would expect an inbound rule allowing port 8080 from client-sg, rather than opening the port to the whole VPC. I would also confirm EC2-A's security group permits the outbound connection.

Then I would check the NACLs on both subnets because they are stateless, so both the request and return traffic must be allowed. If the AWS network controls look correct, I would test from EC2-A with curl or nc and verify on EC2-B that the application is actually listening on port 8080 and that the operating-system firewall is not blocking it.

If it still fails, I would use VPC Flow Logs to see whether AWS is accepting or rejecting the traffic. That tells me whether I should continue at the AWS network layer or move to the operating system and application layer.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc, aws_subnet, aws_route_table, aws_route_table_association, aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule, optional aws_network_acl/aws_network_acl_rule

Resource relationships

Both subnets inherit the VPC local route for 10.0.0.0/16. EC2-A uses client-sg and EC2-B uses app-sg; app-sg references client-sg on TCP 8080. No NAT Gateway, Internet Gateway or peering route belongs in this path.

Production pattern

Express east-west trust with SG-to-SG references instead of broad CIDRs. Keep custom NACLs simple unless there is a specific subnet-boundary requirement, because they add stateless return-path complexity.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_security_group" "client" {
  name   = "client-sg"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  name   = "app-sg"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "app_8080" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.client.id
  ip_protocol = "tcp"
  from_port   = 8080
  to_port     = 8080
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "client_to_vpc" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.client.id
  cidr_ipv4         = aws_vpc.main.cidr_block
  ip_protocol       = "-1"
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Before changing security, confirm EC2-B is listening on 8080 and that the destination ENI has app-sg attached. Review subnet NACL associations and Flow Logs if the SG path is correct.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Connection to 10.0.12.20:8080 fails
1. Is EC2-B healthy and reachable at the OS level?
2. Is the application listening on :8080? ss -lntp
3. Does app-sg allow TCP 8080 from client-sg?
4. Does client-sg allow the outbound connection?
5. Are both private IPs inside the same VPC CIDR?
6. Does the route table contain 10.0.0.0/16 → local?
7. Do both subnet NACLs allow request and return traffic?
8. Check VPC Flow Logs: ACCEPT or REJECT?
9. If Flow Logs show ACCEPT, inspect OS firewall and application binding/listener.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Private east-west traffic
EC2 instances in the same VPC communicate using private IPs over the AWS VPC network.
Local routing
The VPC local route connects its subnets, including across Availability Zones. No NAT or IGW is required.
Least privilege
Using client-sg → app-sg is tighter and easier to maintain than allowing the entire VPC CIDR.
Layered control
Security Groups are the primary stateful workload firewall; NACLs are optional stateless subnet guardrails.
Q4L1SG / NACL
SCENARIO

A TCP request reaches an application, but the response traffic never gets back to the client after a network-hardening change. How would you distinguish Security Group behavior from a NACL problem?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
A TCP request reaches an application, but the response traffic never gets back to the client after a network-hardening change. How would you distinguish Security Group behavior from a NACL problem
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNETWORKING
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use Security Groups for workload trust and NACLs only where subnet-level guardrails are justified; Flow Logs provide network acceptance/rejection evidence.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
EC2-A → client-sg → Subnet-A NACL → VPC local route → Subnet-B NACL → app-sg → EC2-B:8080; return traffic crosses both NACLs again.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Security Groups are stateful
  • NACLs are stateless
  • Allow service port in request direction
  • Allow ephemeral return ports in the reverse NACL direction
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would use Security Groups as the primary workload firewall and express trust between tiers, for example ALB-SG on 443, APP-SG allowing the application port only from ALB-SG, and DB-SG allowing the database port only from APP-SG. I would keep NACLs as coarse subnet-level stateless controls, not as a replacement for SGs. This creates clear least-privilege boundaries while preserving stateful return traffic at the SG layer.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule/egress_rule, aws_network_acl, aws_network_acl_rule, aws_network_acl_association

Resource relationships

Security Groups are stateful ENI controls; NACLs are stateless subnet controls. If a custom NACL permits the request port but blocks ephemeral return ports, the request can reach the application while the response is dropped at the subnet boundary.

Production pattern

Use SGs as the primary workload firewall. Use NACLs only where subnet-level allow/deny is required, define both directions explicitly, and manage rule numbers from a deterministic map to avoid collisions.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "app_in" {
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.app.id
  rule_number    = 100
  egress         = false
  protocol       = "6"
  rule_action    = "allow"
  cidr_block     = var.client_cidr
  from_port = 8080
  to_port   = 8080
}
resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "return_out" {
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.app.id
  rule_number    = 110
  egress         = true
  protocol       = "6"
  rule_action    = "allow"
  cidr_block     = var.client_cidr
  from_port = 1024
  to_port   = 65535
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Treat NACL changes as network changes with blast-radius review. Test both request and return directions and inspect Flow Logs before widening rules. Never “fix” a stateless return issue by opening all ports globally.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. Wrong SG attached
  2. Wrong source SG/CIDR or port
  3. NACL rule order
  4. Ephemeral return ports blocked
  5. Flow Logs ACCEPT but app still failing
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
SG-to-SG rules provide least-privilege workload trust while preserving stateful return traffic. NACLs add coarse stateless subnet controls but increase operational complexity if overused.
Q5L1DNS
SCENARIO

An instance can reach known IP addresses, but DNS names suddenly stop resolving. Network routes were not intentionally changed. How would you troubleshoot this without guessing?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
An instance can reach known IP addresses, but DNS names suddenly stop resolving. Network routes were not intentionally changed. How would you troubleshoot this without guessing?
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionDNS
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
When IP connectivity works but names fail, the investigation should move to resolver choice, zone/rule association and DNS transport rather than NAT/IGW.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Client/workload → Route 53 Resolver → Hosted zone / Resolver rule → Selected DNS answer → Destination
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Correct record exists
  • PHZ associated with affected VPC
  • Resolver rule associated to VPC
  • UDP/TCP 53 reaches on-prem DNS
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

If IP connectivity works but DNS names fail, routing is probably not the first problem. I would verify VPC DNS support, the DHCP option set/Resolver path, the relevant private hosted-zone association and the record itself. For hybrid DNS I would check whether the query should enter AWS through a Resolver inbound endpoint or leave AWS through an outbound endpoint and rule. I would test resolution from the affected workload with dig/nslookup, verify UDP/TCP 53 reachability where custom resolvers are involved, and compare the failing name against a known-good name before changing routes.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route53_zone, aws_route53_record, aws_route53_resolver_endpoint, aws_route53_resolver_rule, aws_route53_resolver_rule_association, aws_security_group, VPC DNS attributes

Resource relationships

For AmazonProvidedDNS, VPC DNS support/hostnames must be enabled. For hybrid names, application VPCs associate forwarding rules that send matching domains to outbound Resolver endpoints; inbound endpoints serve queries arriving from on-prem DNS. Resolver ENIs use SGs that permit DNS UDP/TCP 53 from approved resolver networks.

Production pattern

Centralize hybrid Resolver endpoints in a networking account/VPC and share forwarding rules to spokes. Keep private hosted zones and forwarding rules non-overlapping and document precedence.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route53_resolver_endpoint" "outbound" {
  name      = "central-outbound"
  direction = "OUTBOUND"
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.resolver.id]
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.resolver_a.id }
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.resolver_b.id }
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule" "corp" {
  domain_name          = "corp.example.com"
  rule_type            = "FORWARD"
  resolver_endpoint_id = aws_route53_resolver_endpoint.outbound.id
  target_ip { ip = var.onprem_dns_1 }
  target_ip { ip = var.onprem_dns_2 }
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule_association" "app" {
  resolver_rule_id = aws_route53_resolver_rule.corp.id
  vpc_id           = aws_vpc.app.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Validate with dig/nslookup against the intended name, Resolver query logs where enabled, SG/NACL rules for UDP/TCP 53, and rule/PHZ associations. Do not change NAT/IGW when raw IP connectivity already works.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. Wrong hosted zone/record
  2. VPC DNS support/Resolver path
  3. PHZ not associated
  4. Resolver rule/direction wrong
  5. UDP/TCP 53 blocked to custom resolver
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

When direct IP connectivity works but names fail, the underlying network path is largely proven. The architecture separates DNS resolution into Route 53 Resolver, private hosted-zone association, and—when hybrid DNS is involved—Resolver rules/endpoints and the VPN/DX path. That keeps DNS troubleshooting focused instead of changing unrelated NAT or IGW routing.

Q6L1SUBNET / IGW
SCENARIO

A new subnet was intended to be public. The VPC has an Internet Gateway, but instances in that subnet still have no direct internet connectivity. What would you verify?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
A new subnet was intended to be public. The VPC has an Internet Gateway, but instances in that subnet still have no direct internet connectivity. What would you verify
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionIGW
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Public reachability requires the complete chain: public IP + subnet route to IGW + security controls + application listener.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Internet ↔ Internet Gateway ↔ public-subnet route table ↔ EC2 public IPv4/ENI ↔ SG/NACL ↔ application listener.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Subnet route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
  • EC2 has public IPv4/EIP where direct internet reachability is required
  • SG/NACL permit the intended flow
  • Application listens on the expected port
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

An Internet Gateway being attached to the VPC does not automatically make a subnet public. I would first check which route table is associated with the new subnet and verify that it contains 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW. Then I would confirm that the instance has a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP, that the security group allows the required inbound port, that the NACL permits the request and return traffic, and that the application is actually listening. If another public subnet works, I would compare its route-table association and network controls with this subnet.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_subnet, aws_internet_gateway, aws_route_table, aws_route, aws_route_table_association, aws_instance/launch_template, aws_security_group

Resource relationships

A subnet is public because its associated route table has 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW. Directly internet-reachable EC2 also needs public addressing and security/listener configuration.

Production pattern

Create explicit public/private route tables and associations. Avoid relying on the VPC main route table for tier classification.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_subnet" "public_a" {
  vpc_id                  = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block              = "10.0.1.0/24"
  availability_zone       = var.az_a
  map_public_ip_on_launch = true
}
resource "aws_route_table" "public" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }
resource "aws_route" "internet" {
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.public.id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  gateway_id             = aws_internet_gateway.main.id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "public_a" {
  subnet_id = aws_subnet.public_a.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Use tests/preconditions to ensure public subnets have IGW routes and private subnets do not. Prefer ALB/NAT in public subnets and keep application nodes private.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

A subnet is classified as public by its routing, not by the existence of an IGW in the VPC. Keeping explicit public-subnet route-table associations makes the internet boundary easy to audit and prevents private workloads from accidentally inheriting public routing.

Q7L1SOURCE CONTROL
SCENARIO

HTTPS to the same EC2 service works from the corporate network but fails from a newly added office CIDR. How would you compare the two network paths and controls?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
HTTPS to the same EC2 service works from the corporate network but fails from a newly added office CIDR. How would you compare the two network paths and controls
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNETWORKING
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use Security Groups for workload trust and NACLs only where subnet-level guardrails are justified; Flow Logs provide network acceptance/rejection evidence.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Source network → VPC/Internet path → subnet NACL → EC2 Security Group → EC2 listener; compare the allowed and failing source CIDRs.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Correct source CIDR or source SG
  • Correct destination port (22/443)
  • NACL request and return rules
  • Route path and application listener
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Because the same EC2 service works from one source network but not another, I would compare the two source paths rather than starting with the instance itself. I would verify the source CIDRs seen by AWS, then check the EC2 security-group rules for TCP 22 or 443 and make sure the failing source CIDR is intentionally allowed. I would also check the subnet NACL and any upstream firewall, proxy, VPN, or corporate egress NAT that may cause the real source IP to differ from what I expect. VPC Flow Logs would help confirm whether AWS is rejecting the failing source.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule, optional aws_network_acl_rule, route resources for VPN/DX/TGW path

Resource relationships

The new office CIDR must be represented consistently across routing and security. The workload SG allows HTTPS from the approved office range; custom NACLs and hybrid/TGW routes must also contain the new prefix in both required directions.

Production pattern

Model approved source CIDRs as version-controlled inputs or managed prefix lists so the same authoritative set feeds routes and security rules.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "corp" {
  name           = "corp-office-cidrs"
  address_family = "IPv4"
  max_entries    = 20
  entry {
    cidr        = "10.50.0.0/16"
    description = "HQ"
  }
  entry {
    cidr        = var.new_office_cidr
    description = "Office-B"
  }
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "https_corp" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.web.id
  prefix_list_id    = aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list.corp.id
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Compare the working and failing source CIDRs in effective routes, SG rules, NACLs and on-prem firewall policy. Roll out new prefixes with review because an incorrect supernet can broaden access.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

Source-specific SG rules enforce least privilege at the workload boundary. Comparing a working source with a failing source is also a fast way to isolate whether the issue is AWS policy, source NAT, an upstream network control, or the application.

Q8L1SECURITY GROUP
SCENARIO

The Security Group appears to allow the required port, but the connection still times out. What else do you verify before changing the SG again?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SECURITY EVENT
The Security Group appears to allow the required port, but the connection still times out. What else do you verify before changing the SG again
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionSECURITY
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use Security Groups for workload trust and NACLs only where subnet-level guardrails are justified; Flow Logs provide network acceptance/rejection evidence.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Source → route table → subnet NACL → destination Security Group → ENI → host firewall/application listener.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Confirm the SG is attached to the correct ENI
  • Check route and NACL in both directions
  • Check OS firewall and bind/listen address
  • Use Flow Logs to separate AWS-network rejection from application failure
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

If the security-group rule appears correct but the connection still times out, I would verify that the expected SG is actually attached to the correct ENI and that the rule matches the real source, destination port, and protocol. Then I would inspect the subnet NACLs, route tables, and return path. If the VPC network controls look correct, I would check whether the application is listening on the expected address/port and whether the OS firewall is blocking it. VPC Flow Logs are useful here: a REJECT keeps me in the network-control layer, while ACCEPT pushes the investigation toward the host or application.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule/egress_rule, aws_route_table/route/association, optional aws_network_acl_rule, aws_flow_log

Resource relationships

The SG is only one control in the path. Terraform should model the subnet route association, next hop, NACL policy and destination SG separately so a correct SG does not hide a routing or host/listener failure.

Production pattern

Keep networking layers as separate resources/modules with explicit outputs. Troubleshooting changes should be evidence-led; do not widen SGs as a generic test.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "app" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.client.id
  ip_protocol = "tcp"
  from_port = var.app_port
  to_port   = var.app_port
}
resource "aws_flow_log" "vpc" {
  vpc_id          = aws_vpc.main.id
  traffic_type    = "ALL"
  log_destination = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.flow.arn
  iam_role_arn    = aws_iam_role.flow_logs.arn
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify route target/association, NACL, destination ENI SG attachment, listener/host firewall and Flow Logs before changing SG policy. Keep emergency changes in Terraform and reconcile state immediately.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. Recent deployment/configuration change
  2. IAM/security boundary
  3. Network/DNS dependency
  4. Capacity/quota/health signal
  5. Application or downstream dependency
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

Security Groups are stateful, but they are only one layer in the path. Routing, NACLs, ENI attachment, the host firewall, and the application listener can independently cause a timeout, so the diagram keeps those layers separate.

Q9L1NACL
SCENARIO

A NACL change causes intermittent connection failures even though Security Groups were untouched. Explain how you would prove whether the stateless return path is the issue.

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
A NACL change causes intermittent connection failures even though Security Groups were untouched. Explain how you would prove whether the stateless return path is the issue
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNACL
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use Security Groups for workload trust and NACLs only where subnet-level guardrails are justified; Flow Logs provide network acceptance/rejection evidence.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
EC2-A → SG → Subnet-A NACL → route → Subnet-B NACL → SG → EC2-B; the return path must satisfy stateless NACL rules as well.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • NACL rule order
  • Inbound and outbound rules
  • Ephemeral return-port range
  • Compare last known-good NACL from Terraform/CloudTrail
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would use Security Groups as the primary workload firewall and express trust between tiers, for example ALB-SG on 443, APP-SG allowing the application port only from ALB-SG, and DB-SG allowing the database port only from APP-SG. I would keep NACLs as coarse subnet-level stateless controls, not as a replacement for SGs. This creates clear least-privilege boundaries while preserving stateful return traffic at the SG layer.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_network_acl, aws_network_acl_rule, aws_network_acl_association, aws_flow_log, aws_security_group

Resource relationships

A custom NACL needs explicit request and return rules. For TCP clients, the return path normally requires the client-side ephemeral port range; the exact range depends on client OS/application behavior.

Production pattern

Represent inbound/outbound rules as data and generate them with for_each. Reserve rule-number ranges per purpose to avoid accidental shadowing by lower-numbered deny rules.

Representative Terraform
locals {
  app_nacl = {
    app_in   = { no=100, egress=false, from=8080, to=8080, cidr=var.client_cidr }
    return_o = { no=110, egress=true,  from=1024, to=65535, cidr=var.client_cidr }
  }
}
resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "app" {
  for_each       = local.app_nacl
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.app.id
  rule_number    = each.value.no
  egress         = each.value.egress
  protocol       = "6"
  rule_action    = "allow"
  cidr_block     = each.value.cidr
  from_port      = each.value.from
  to_port        = each.value.to
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Use Flow Logs to compare ACCEPT/REJECT around the NACL change. Do not assume “intermittent” means application instability; ephemeral-port asymmetry is a classic stateless-filter symptom.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
  1. Wrong SG attached
  2. Wrong source SG/CIDR or port
  3. NACL rule order
  4. Ephemeral return ports blocked
  5. Flow Logs ACCEPT but app still failing
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
SG-to-SG rules provide least-privilege workload trust while preserving stateful return traffic. NACLs add coarse stateless subnet controls but increase operational complexity if overused.
Q10L1VPC ENDPOINT
SCENARIO

An S3 VPC endpoint exists, but private workloads still send S3 traffic through the NAT Gateway. What configuration would you inspect, and how would you prove which path is being used?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
An S3 VPC endpoint exists, but private workloads still send S3 traffic through the NAT Gateway. What configuration would you inspect, and how would you prove which path is being used
SCOPE
Multi-AZProductionNAT
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
A gateway endpoint can exist and still be unused if the workload subnet is associated with a route table that does not contain the endpoint prefix-list route.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private workload → private route table → S3 prefix-list route → S3 Gateway Endpoint → Amazon S3. The default 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT remains for other internet destinations.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Gateway endpoint associated with the workload route table
  • S3 prefix-list route present
  • Endpoint and bucket policies allow access
  • NAT remains only for non-endpoint destinations
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would first identify the endpoint type. For an S3 or DynamoDB gateway endpoint, the endpoint must be associated with the route table used by the workload subnet so the service prefix-list route points to the endpoint. If that route-table association is missing, the more general 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT path can still be used. For an interface endpoint, I would instead check private DNS, endpoint ENIs, the endpoint security group, and TCP 443. I would verify the actual workload route table rather than just confirming that an endpoint object exists.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_endpoint (Gateway), aws_route_table, aws_route_table_association, endpoint policy

Resource relationships

An S3 Gateway Endpoint injects an S3 prefix-list route into the route tables listed on the endpoint. Every intended private workload route table must be associated; S3 traffic then takes the endpoint route instead of 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT.

Production pattern

Attach the endpoint to workload route tables from a central set/map. Use an endpoint policy that is restrictive enough for production but not so restrictive that required buckets/actions are blocked.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.${var.region}.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = [for rt in aws_route_table.private : rt.id]
  policy            = data.aws_iam_policy_document.s3_endpoint.json
}
data "aws_iam_policy_document" "s3_endpoint" {
  statement {
    effect = "Allow"
    principals {
      type        = "*"
      identifiers = ["*"]
    }
    actions   = ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:ListBucket"]
    resources = var.allowed_s3_arns
  }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify effective route-table entries for the S3 managed prefix list and test from each subnet. Compare NAT bytes before/after rollout. Treat endpoint policy and bucket policy as independent authorization layers.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

Creating a VPC endpoint does not automatically force workloads to use it. Gateway endpoints depend on the correct route-table association, while interface endpoints depend on ENI placement, private DNS, and security groups. Making those relationships explicit removes unnecessary NAT usage and keeps supported AWS-service traffic private.

Q11L1ROUTE SELECTION
SCENARIO

A subnet route table contains 10.0.0.0/8 → TGW, 10.20.0.0/16 → peering, and 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT. A workload calls 10.20.5.10. Which route wins, and how would you explain AWS route selection in an interview?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
Choose the actual next hop for a destination when multiple routes match.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentROUTE SELECTION
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use longest-prefix match first; then reason about route target/state and whether the selected route is usable.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Workload → associated route table → longest-prefix match (10.20.0.0/16) → peering → destination
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Subnet → correct route-table association
  • 10.20.0.0/16 → peering
  • 10.0.0.0/8 → TGW
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

AWS routing is destination based. I first identify the route table actually associated with the source subnet, then choose the most specific matching prefix. For 10.20.5.10, 10.20.0.0/16 is more specific than 10.0.0.0/8 or 0.0.0.0/0, so the peering route is selected.

After route selection I still validate that the target is healthy/active and that the return path plus SG/NACL controls permit the traffic.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route_table, aws_route for TGW/peering/NAT destinations

Resource relationships

Terraform materializes competing destination prefixes in the subnet route table. AWS selects the most specific matching destination first, so 10.20.0.0/16 wins over 10.0.0.0/8 and 0.0.0.0/0.

Production pattern

Keep destination prefixes explicit and validated. Avoid duplicated ownership of the same route table across stacks.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route" "corp_tgw" {
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/8"
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
resource "aws_route" "service_peer" {
  route_table_id            = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_cidr_block    = "10.20.0.0/16"
  vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.service.id
}
resource "aws_route" "default" {
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.az.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

CI should reject duplicate exact destinations and flag unexpectedly broad prefixes. Review route diffs as high-risk because a more-specific route can redirect traffic without changing the default route.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Identify source subnet and associated route table.
  2. List every route matching the destination.
  3. Apply longest-prefix match.
  4. Validate selected target state and reverse route.
  5. Verify SG/NACL and test from the workload.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It tests whether you understand routing decisions rather than memorizing NAT/IGW diagrams.

Q12L1PEERING vs TGW
SCENARIO

You have three VPCs today and expect twenty within a year. What limitations of VPC Peering would make you consider Transit Gateway instead?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
Explain the scale and routing trade-off between one-to-one peering and a transit hub.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTransit GatewayTerraform-managedProductionPEERING vs TGW
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Peering is non-transitive and becomes operationally complex as a mesh; TGW centralizes transitive routing and segmentation.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
VPCs → Peering mesh (small scale) OR VPC attachments → Transit Gateway → segmented route tables
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Non-overlapping CIDRs
  • Routes on both sides of peering
  • TGW attachments
  • TGW route-table association/propagation
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Peering is useful for a small number of VPCs that need direct private connectivity, but it is non-transitive and the number of connections/routes grows as the estate grows.

For many VPCs or hybrid connectivity, I would consider Transit Gateway because it provides a central transit point and route-table based segmentation. I would still use PrivateLink when consumers need only a specific service rather than broad network connectivity.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_ec2_transit_gateway, aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment, aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table, association/propagation, aws_ram_resource_share for cross-account use

Resource relationships

Spoke VPCs attach to a central TGW; TGW route tables provide controlled transitive connectivity and segmentation. VPC route tables point required remote prefixes to TGW; TGW association/propagation controls which segments learn each other.

Production pattern

For growth beyond a small mesh, separate prod/non-prod/shared-services TGW route tables and share the TGW through RAM/Organizations. Do not enable default association/propagation blindly in a segmented estate.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway" "core" {
  default_route_table_association = "disable"
  default_route_table_propagation = "disable"
}
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "app" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  vpc_id             = aws_vpc.app.id
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.tgw_a.id, aws_subnet.tgw_b.id]
}
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_association" "app" {
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.app.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Model TGW core routing in a central network stack; application stacks should only request approved attachments/segments. Validate segmentation with route-table inspection and connectivity tests.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

This is an architecture-choice question, not a service-definition question.

Q13L1VPN vs DX
SCENARIO

A team asks whether they should use Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect for hybrid connectivity. What questions do you ask before choosing?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
Choose hybrid connectivity from latency, throughput, resilience, encryption, lead-time, and cost requirements.
SCOPE
Multi-AZDirect ConnectVPNTerraform-managedVPN vs DX
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
VPN is internet-based and quick to deploy; DX provides dedicated private connectivity but still needs an HA design and often VPN as backup.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
On-prem router → VPN over internet OR DX circuit → AWS gateway/TGW → VPC
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • BGP/static routing design
  • Redundant tunnels/circuits
  • DX gateway/TGW/VGW choice
  • Failover preference and route advertisements
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would ask about bandwidth, latency consistency, availability target, encryption requirements, time to provision, locations, and cost. VPN is quick and encrypted over the public internet; Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity and more consistent network characteristics.

For production I would not treat one DX circuit as HA. I would design diverse connectivity and test a VPN or secondary DX path according to the business requirement.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_customer_gateway, aws_vpn_connection/aws_vpn_gateway or TGW attachment; aws_dx_gateway, DX virtual interface/association where managed

Resource relationships

VPN supplies encrypted internet-based hybrid connectivity; DX supplies private dedicated connectivity but not encryption by itself. Both ultimately need compatible AWS and on-prem routing/BGP plus redundant devices/paths.

Production pattern

Use Terraform for AWS-side gateways, attachments and routing. Treat carrier cross-connects, BGP policy and on-prem router config as coordinated external dependencies rather than pretending Terraform alone creates the circuit.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_customer_gateway" "onprem" {
  bgp_asn    = var.onprem_asn
  ip_address = var.onprem_public_ip
  type       = "ipsec.1"
}
resource "aws_vpn_connection" "backup" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.onprem.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
  static_routes_only  = false
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Choose based on bandwidth/latency/lead time/resiliency/encryption/compliance. For DX, plan redundant connections/locations and a VPN backup; test failover rather than assuming BGP policy is correct.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

Real interviews test requirements and trade-offs, not just the definition of VPN or DX.

Q14L1IPV6 EGRESS
SCENARIO

A private subnet is dual stack. IPv4 internet egress uses a NAT Gateway. What is the equivalent design for outbound-only IPv6, and why is it different?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
Explain dual-stack egress without assuming IPv6 requires address translation.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedProductionIPV6 EGRESS
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Use ::/0 → egress-only Internet Gateway for outbound-only IPv6; NAT Gateway remains relevant to private IPv4 egress.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
IPv6 workload → route table ::/0 → egress-only IGW → internet
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • IPv6 CIDR on VPC/subnet
  • ::/0 → egress-only IGW
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT for IPv4
  • SG/NACL rules for IPv6
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

IPv6 addresses are globally routable, so I do not use NAT just to hide private addresses. For outbound-only IPv6 from a private subnet I use an egress-only Internet Gateway and route ::/0 to it.

IPv4 private egress can continue through a NAT Gateway. Security Groups and NACLs still need explicit IPv6 rules where appropriate.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc IPv6 CIDR association, aws_subnet ipv6_cidr_block, aws_egress_only_internet_gateway, aws_route

Resource relationships

Private IPv6 workloads do not use NAT Gateway. Their ::/0 route can target an egress-only IGW, which permits outbound-initiated IPv6 connectivity while blocking unsolicited inbound initiation.

Production pattern

Design dual stack intentionally: IPv4 private egress via NAT/endpoints; IPv6 outbound-only via egress-only IGW. Apply IPv6 SG rules explicitly because IPv4 CIDRs do not cover IPv6.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_egress_only_internet_gateway" "this" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_route" "private_ipv6" {
  route_table_id              = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_ipv6_cidr_block = "::/0"
  egress_only_gateway_id      = aws_egress_only_internet_gateway.this.id
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "https_v6" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
  cidr_ipv6         = "::/0"
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port = 443
  to_port   = 443
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify IPv6 addressing, ::/0 route, SG IPv6 rules and DNS AAAA behavior. Do not assume NAT Gateway protects IPv6; it is not in the IPv6 path.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It verifies that you understand the fundamental addressing difference between IPv4 NAT and IPv6 egress control.

Q15L1FLOW LOGS
SCENARIO

What can VPC Flow Logs prove during a connectivity incident, and what can they not prove? Give a production example.

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
REQUIREMENT
Use Flow Logs as network evidence without over-interpreting ACCEPT/REJECT.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentFLOW LOGS
DESIGN DECISION / PRIMARY CHECK
Flow Logs show metadata about flows and acceptance/rejection at captured interfaces; they do not prove application success or replace packet/application logs.
Current / Check ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
ENI / subnet / VPC traffic → Flow Logs → CloudWatch Logs or S3 → investigation
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Correct capture scope
  • Traffic type ALL/ACCEPT/REJECT
  • Log destination/permissions
  • Fields needed for source/destination/ports/action
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I use Flow Logs to see who talked to whom, on which protocol/ports, and whether the flow was accepted or rejected at the captured network interface. They are excellent for narrowing scope.

An ACCEPT record does not prove the application completed a request. The process may not be listening, the OS firewall may block it, TLS may fail, or the application may time out later. I correlate Flow Logs with host, load-balancer, and application evidence.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_flow_log, aws_cloudwatch_log_group or S3 destination, aws_iam_role/policy for CloudWatch delivery, optional Athena/Firehose pipeline

Resource relationships

Flow Logs attach to VPC/subnet/ENI scope and publish IP/port/action metadata. They provide network-flow evidence but do not show application payload, process/listener state or all intermediate service behavior.

Production pattern

Enable at least VPC-level Flow Logs centrally, with structured fields and retention aligned to incident/compliance needs. Use S3 for long retention/analytics and CloudWatch for fast operational queries when appropriate.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_flow_log" "vpc" {
  vpc_id               = aws_vpc.main.id
  traffic_type         = "ALL"
  log_destination_type = "s3"
  log_destination      = aws_s3_bucket.flow_logs.arn
  max_aggregation_interval = 60
  destination_options {
    file_format        = "parquet"
    per_hour_partition = true
  }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Encrypt/log-protect the destination and set lifecycle retention. Use Flow Logs as one evidence source alongside ALB/NLB logs, host metrics and application telemetry.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Locate the relevant ENI/subnet/VPC.
  2. Filter by source/destination/port/time.
  3. Interpret ACCEPT/REJECT cautiously.
  4. Correlate with route/security configuration.
  5. Continue to OS/application evidence when network acceptance is proven.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

SRE interviews look for evidence quality and scope, not a one-tool answer.

L2

Production Troubleshooting + Incident Response

30 scenarios
Q16L2ROUTE TABLE
SCENARIO

A Terraform change modifies route-table associations and private workloads immediately lose outbound access. How do you identify the exact bad change, restore service, and avoid creating drift?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A Terraform change modifies route-table associations and private workloads immediately lose outbound access. How do you identify the exact bad change, restore service, and avoid creating drift
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private EC2 → Private RT → NAT Gateway → Public RT → Internet Gateway Compare the failing subnet association and route with the last known-good Terraform state.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Subnet → route-table association
  • 0.0.0.0/0 target
  • NAT subnet/public RT → IGW
  • CloudTrail route-table API changes
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Since the outage started after a route-table change, I would compare the failing private subnet with a known-good subnet first

I would verify the subnet association, confirm its default route points to the intended NAT Gateway, then verify that NAT is in a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW

I would check CloudTrail and the Terraform/Git diff for the exact route or association mutation, use Flow Logs to confirm where packets stop, and roll back the route-table change if customer impact is high

Recovery is verified from an instance in the affected subnet, then I would add plan review/tests that assert each private subnet has the expected same-AZ egress path.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route_table_association, aws_route, Terraform state/backend, CI plan artifact

Resource relationships

The subnet-to-route-table association is the likely control-plane change. Recovery should restore the intended association through the owning Terraform state, not by leaving an untracked console fix.

Production pattern

Separate shared network state from app state, require saved plans/approval for route changes, and use versioned modules. If an emergency console rollback is required, immediately import/reconcile it before the next apply.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route_table_association" "private" {
  for_each       = var.private_subnets
  subnet_id      = each.value.subnet_id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private[each.value.az_key].id
  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = each.value.az_key == aws_route_table.private[each.value.az_key].tags["AzKey"]
      error_message = "Private subnet must use its intended AZ route table."
    }
  }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Compare the applied commit, saved plan and AWS association IDs. Roll back the code/module version through CI, verify service restoration, then run a clean plan showing no unintended drift.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. Since the outage started after a route-table change, I would compare the failing private subnet with a known-good subnet first.
2. I would verify the subnet association, confirm its default route points to the intended NAT Gateway, then verify that NAT is in a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW.
3. I would check CloudTrail and the Terraform/Git diff for the exact route or association mutation, use Flow Logs to confirm where packets stop, and roll back the route-table change if customer impact is high.
4. Recovery is verified from an instance in the affected subnet, then I would add plan review/tests that assert each private subnet has the expected same-AZ egress path.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Compare the failing subnet association and route with the last known-good Terraform state.

Production resources

per-AZ aws_nat_gateway/eip, aws_route_table, aws_route, aws_route_table_association

Resource relationships

Production pattern

Use an AZ-keyed map for subnet, route table and NAT resources so Terraform relationships encode the availability-domain intent.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route" "private_default" {
  for_each               = local.azs
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private[each.key].id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.az[each.key].id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "private" {
  for_each       = local.azs
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.private[each.key].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private[each.key].id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Gate changes on a topology test that asserts subnet-A→RT-A→NAT-A and subnet-B→RT-B→NAT-B. Verify egress from one test workload per AZ after apply.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. Because only one AZ is affected, I would not troubleshoot the whole VPC.
2. I would compare AZ-B against the working AZ-A path: private subnet association, 0.0.0.0/0 route, NAT-B state and placement, public subnet route to the IGW, NACLs and DNS.
3. NAT-B being Available does not prove the workload is actually routing to it.
4. I would inspect the Terraform diff and CloudTrail for route-table association changes, then restore the last known-good same-AZ path and verify egress from AZ-B.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Because AZ-A works, compare AZ-B against the healthy same-AZ path instead of troubleshooting the whole VPC.
Q18L2NAT COST
SCENARIO

NAT Gateway data-processing charges double in a week even though application request volume is flat. How would you find the traffic causing the increase and redesign the path if necessary?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
NAT Gateway data-processing charges double in a week even though application request volume is flat. How would you find the traffic causing the increase and redesign the path if necessary
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private workload → route table → VPC endpoint for supported AWS services; only true internet destinations continue through NAT Gateway → IGW.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Identify NAT bytes by destination/service
  • Add S3 gateway endpoint where appropriate
  • Add required interface endpoints such as ECR API/DKR
  • Keep same-AZ NAT for residual internet egress
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would first identify which source subnets and destinations are driving NAT bytes using Cost Explorer/CUR, NAT metrics and VPC Flow Logs

A common cause is AWS-service traffic such as S3 or ECR being sent through NAT after an endpoint or route change

I would confirm whether supported gateway/interface endpoints exist and are actually selected by route tables and private DNS

I would not remove NAT blindly; I would move high-volume supported service traffic to endpoints, verify functionality, and then confirm the NAT data-processing trend falls.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_nat_gateway, aws_vpc_endpoint, route tables, aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm, optional CUR/Athena outside Terraform networking stack

Resource relationships

High-volume S3/DynamoDB traffic can move to Gateway Endpoints; many other AWS APIs can use Interface Endpoints. Keeping traffic private reduces NAT processing bytes and often cross-AZ transfer when endpoints/NAT are placed correctly.

Production pattern

Baseline NAT BytesOutToDestination/BytesInFromSource and Cost Explorer/CUR, identify top destinations, then add endpoints only where volume/security justify hourly endpoint costs.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.${var.region}.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = local.private_route_table_ids
}
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "nat_bytes" {
  alarm_name          = "nat-unexpected-byte-growth"
  namespace           = "AWS/NATGateway"
  metric_name         = "BytesOutToDestination"
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 300
  evaluation_periods  = 3
  threshold           = var.nat_byte_alarm_threshold
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
  dimensions = { NatGatewayId = aws_nat_gateway.az["a"].id }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Measure before and after. Do not remove NAT until every required non-endpoint internet dependency is understood. Keep endpoints in the same AZs as consumers where applicable.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. I would first identify which source subnets and destinations are driving NAT bytes using Cost Explorer/CUR, NAT metrics and VPC Flow Logs.
2. A common cause is AWS-service traffic such as S3 or ECR being sent through NAT after an endpoint or route change.
3. I would confirm whether supported gateway/interface endpoints exist and are actually selected by route tables and private DNS.
4. I would not remove NAT blindly; I would move high-volume supported service traffic to endpoints, verify functionality, and then confirm the NAT data-processing trend falls.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Use VPC endpoints for supported AWS services and keep NAT for destinations that actually require internet egress.
Q19L2ECR / ENDPOINTS
SCENARIO
