Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
After removing NAT Gateways from private subnets, EKS nodes can no longer pull images from ECR and some workloads cannot reach S3. What private connectivity is missing
SCOPE
Multi-AZPrivate subnetS3Terraform-managedPost-Terraform change
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private EKS/EC2 → DNS / Routes → VPC Endpoints → AWS Services ECR image pulls commonly need ECR API, ECR DKR and S3 access; removing NAT before all required endpoints exist breaks pulls.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Private DNS enabled
  • Endpoint SG allows TCP 443
  • S3 prefix list → gateway endpoint
  • Associated with workload route tables
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Removing NAT is safe only after every required private service path exists

For S3 I would expect a gateway endpoint associated with the private route tables

For ECR, I would check the ECR API and ECR DKR interface endpoints, their security groups/private DNS, and the S3 path used for image layers

I would compare DNS resolution and endpoint reachability from the failing subnet, restore NAT temporarily if production is blocked, then complete the endpoint set and retest before removing NAT again.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_endpoint for ecr.api, ecr.dkr, s3 Gateway, sts/logs/ec2 as required; endpoint SG; private route tables; aws_eks_cluster/node groups

Resource relationships

Private EKS nodes need ECR API + ECR DKR Interface Endpoints and S3 access for image layers. Depending on workloads/bootstrap they may also need STS, CloudWatch Logs, EC2, SSM and other service endpoints. Interface endpoints require private DNS and SG access from node/pod networks.

Production pattern

Define required AWS service endpoints from a service map and deploy interface endpoints across workload AZs. Use an S3 Gateway Endpoint on all private route tables.

Representative Terraform
locals {
  interface_services = toset(["ecr.api","ecr.dkr","sts","logs"])
}
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "interface" {
  for_each            = local.interface_services
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.${var.region}.${each.key}"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = local.private_subnet_ids
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.vpce.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.${var.region}.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = local.private_route_table_ids
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Test a fresh image pull, STS call and log delivery from private nodes after NAT isolation. Maintain an explicit dependency inventory so “no NAT” does not become “no path to an unmodeled service.”

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. Removing NAT is safe only after every required private service path exists.
2. For S3 I would expect a gateway endpoint associated with the private route tables.
3. For ECR, I would check the ECR API and ECR DKR interface endpoints, their security groups/private DNS, and the S3 path used for image layers.
4. I would compare DNS resolution and endpoint reachability from the failing subnet, restore NAT temporarily if production is blocked, then complete the endpoint set and retest before removing NAT again.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
ECR image pulls commonly need ECR API, ECR DKR and S3 access; removing NAT before all required endpoints exist breaks pulls.
Q20L2INTERFACE ENDPOINT
SCENARIO

An Interface VPC Endpoint resolves to private IPs, but connections to the service are refused or time out. Which layers do you check?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
An Interface VPC Endpoint resolves to private IPs, but connections to the service are refused or time out. Which layers do you check
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private EC2 → Private DNS → Endpoint ENI → Endpoint SG → AWS Service Successful DNS resolution proves name mapping, not that the endpoint security group or service policy permits the connection.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Private DNS → endpoint ENI IP
  • Resolution working narrows fault to transport/policy
  • Endpoint SG allows 443 from workload SG/CIDR
  • Endpoint + IAM policy allow action
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

If the service name resolves to the interface endpoint but the connection is refused or times out, DNS has already done its job

I would check the endpoint ENI security group for the service port from the workload source, then the workload SG egress, endpoint policy/service policy and subnet NACLs

I would verify which endpoint ENI IP the client resolves and test TCP 443 directly

If a recent Terraform change altered the endpoint SG or subnet associations, I would revert that specific change and verify the private connection.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_endpoint Interface, aws_security_group, aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule, subnets, private DNS

Resource relationships

An Interface Endpoint creates ENIs with private IPs in selected subnets. Clients resolve the service name to those IPs when private DNS is enabled; the endpoint SG must allow TCP 443 from approved clients, and client egress/NACLs must permit the path.

Production pattern

Use a dedicated endpoint SG, multi-AZ endpoint ENIs, private DNS and explicit endpoint policies where supported. Avoid reusing broad application SGs.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_security_group" "vpce" {
  name   = "vpce-https"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "vpce_https" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.vpce.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
  ip_protocol = "tcp"
  from_port   = 443
  to_port     = 443
}
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "service" {
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name        = var.service_name
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = local.private_subnet_ids
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.vpce.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify DNS returns endpoint ENI IPs, endpoint SG allows 443, and endpoint policy/IAM authorization permits the API call. Endpoint “Available” alone does not prove application reachability.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. If the service name resolves to the interface endpoint but the connection is refused or times out, DNS has already done its job.
2. I would check the endpoint ENI security group for the service port from the workload source, then the workload SG egress, endpoint policy/service policy and subnet NACLs.
3. I would verify which endpoint ENI IP the client resolves and test TCP 443 directly.
4. If a recent Terraform change altered the endpoint SG or subnet associations, I would revert that specific change and verify the private connection.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Successful DNS resolution proves name mapping, not that the endpoint security group or service policy permits the connection.
Q21L2GATEWAY ENDPOINT
SCENARIO

An S3 Gateway Endpoint works from private subnet A but not private subnet B. Both subnets are in the same VPC. What would you compare first?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
An S3 Gateway Endpoint works from private subnet A but not private subnet B. Both subnets are in the same VPC. What would you compare first
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Subnet A → RT-A → S3 Gateway EP → RT-B → Subnet B Gateway endpoints are attached to route tables; compare the route-table associations for the working and failing subnets.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • 10.0.0.0/16 → local
  • pl-xxxx (S3) → vpce-gw
  • Restrict allowed buckets/actions
  • Combine with IAM least privilege
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

A gateway endpoint working from one subnet but not another strongly suggests a route-table difference

I would identify the route table associated with each subnet and verify that the failing subnet's route table is associated with the gateway endpoint, which installs the service prefix-list route

I would also check the endpoint policy and S3 bucket policy for source VPC/endpoint restrictions

I would fix the missing route-table association in Terraform, apply, and verify from the previously failing subnet.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_endpoint Gateway, aws_route_table list/associations, endpoint policy

Resource relationships

Gateway Endpoint routing is per route table. If subnet A works and B fails, compare which route table each subnet is actually associated with and whether both IDs are attached to the endpoint.

Production pattern

Derive gateway endpoint route_table_ids from the same canonical private-route-table collection used by subnet associations.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.${var.region}.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = values(aws_route_table.private)[*].id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "private" {
  for_each       = local.private_subnets
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.private[each.key].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private[each.value.az_key].id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

After apply, inspect the S3 prefix-list route in every intended private route table and run an S3 call from each AZ/subnet. Validate endpoint and bucket policies separately.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. A gateway endpoint working from one subnet but not another strongly suggests a route-table difference.
2. I would identify the route table associated with each subnet and verify that the failing subnet's route table is associated with the gateway endpoint, which installs the service prefix-list route.
3. I would also check the endpoint policy and S3 bucket policy for source VPC/endpoint restrictions.
4. I would fix the missing route-table association in Terraform, apply, and verify from the previously failing subnet.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Gateway endpoints are attached to route tables; compare the route-table associations for the working and failing subnets.
Q22L2VPC PEERING
SCENARIO

A VPC peering connection is Active, but applications in the two VPCs still cannot communicate. What does Active prove, and what does it not prove?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A VPC peering connection is Active, but applications in the two VPCs still cannot communicate. What does Active prove, and what does it not prove
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
VPC-A App → RT-A → Peering pcx → RT-B → VPC-B App Peering needs routes on both sides plus SG/NACL permission; an Active peering connection alone does not create reachability.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • 10.20.0.0/16 → pcx
  • 10.10.0.0/16 → pcx
  • CIDRs do not overlap
  • Routes exist on both sides
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

An Active peering connection only tells me the peering object exists

I would verify non-overlapping CIDRs, then check both VPC route tables: VPC-A needs a route for VPC-B's CIDR through the peering connection and VPC-B needs the return route to VPC-A

Then I would verify SG/NACL rules and test using private IPs

If Terraform recently changed routes, I would compare both sides and restore the missing prefix rather than recreating the peering connection.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_peering_connection, aws_vpc_peering_connection_accepter (cross-account), aws_route in both VPCs, SG rules

Resource relationships

Peering Active means the control-plane connection exists. Reachability still requires non-overlapping CIDRs, routes in both directions, security controls, DNS settings if needed, and a listening destination.

Production pattern

Keep both sides of the peering route intent managed and reviewed. For cross-account peering, split requester/accepter ownership cleanly.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "ab" {
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.a.id
  peer_vpc_id = aws_vpc.b.id
  peer_owner_id = var.peer_account_id
}
resource "aws_route" "a_to_b" {
  route_table_id            = aws_route_table.a_private.id
  destination_cidr_block    = aws_vpc.b.cidr_block
  vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.ab.id
}
resource "aws_route" "b_to_a" {
  provider                  = aws.peer
  route_table_id            = aws_route_table.b_private.id
  destination_cidr_block    = aws_vpc.a.cidr_block
  vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.ab.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify both directions and prevent overlapping CIDRs through IPAM/policy. Do not use peering as a transitive hub; migrate to TGW when topology/segmentation requirements justify it.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. An Active peering connection only tells me the peering object exists.
2. I would verify non-overlapping CIDRs, then check both VPC route tables: VPC-A needs a route for VPC-B's CIDR through the peering connection and VPC-B needs the return route to VPC-A.
3. Then I would verify SG/NACL rules and test using private IPs.
4. If Terraform recently changed routes, I would compare both sides and restore the missing prefix rather than recreating the peering connection.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Peering needs routes on both sides plus SG/NACL permission; an Active peering connection alone does not create reachability.
Q23L2PEERING LIMIT
SCENARIO

VPC-A can reach VPC-B and VPC-B can reach VPC-C, but VPC-A cannot reach VPC-C. Why, and what architecture would you use if transitive connectivity is required?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
VPC-A can reach VPC-B and VPC-B can reach VPC-C, but VPC-A cannot reach VPC-C. Why, and what architecture would you use if transitive connectivity is required
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
VPC-A → Peering A-B → VPC-B → Peering B-C → VPC-C There is no implicit A → B → C transit path. Use direct peering where small, or Transit Gateway when transitive hub routing is required.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • VPC peering is non-transitive
  • A↔B and B↔C does not create A↔C
  • Create explicit A↔C peering for small topology
  • Use TGW for scalable transitive hub routing
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

This is expected behavior for VPC peering: it is not transitive

A can communicate with B and B with C, but B cannot act as a transit router so A does not automatically gain a path to C

I would confirm there is no direct A-C peering or other transit service

If A and C genuinely need connectivity, I would either add direct peering for a small topology or redesign around Transit Gateway for scalable transitive routing.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_ec2_transit_gateway, VPC attachments, TGW route tables, associations/propagations, VPC routes

Resource relationships

VPC peering is non-transitive, so A→B and B→C do not create A→C. TGW provides the explicit transit hop and route tables decide which spokes may communicate.

Production pattern

Migrate from peering mesh to TGW segments with staged routes. Do not leave parallel routes with ambiguous ownership during migration.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table" "shared" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_propagation" "spokes" {
  for_each = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.spoke
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = each.value.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.shared.id
}
resource "aws_route" "to_tgw" {
  for_each               = local.spoke_route_tables
  route_table_id         = each.value
  destination_cidr_block = var.shared_network_cidr
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Test intended and denied spoke-to-spoke paths. Explicitly disable default TGW association/propagation if segmentation matters.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. This is expected behavior for VPC peering: it is not transitive.
2. A can communicate with B and B with C, but B cannot act as a transit router so A does not automatically gain a path to C.
3. I would confirm there is no direct A-C peering or other transit service.
4. If A and C genuinely need connectivity, I would either add direct peering for a small topology or redesign around Transit Gateway for scalable transitive routing.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
There is no implicit A → B → C transit path. Use direct peering where small, or Transit Gateway when transitive hub routing is required.

If connectivity works for some CIDRs but not others, I would treat it as a prefix-specific routing or policy problem rather than an attachment failure

I would trace one working and one failing CIDR through VPC route tables, TGW/peering routes, propagation, return routes and SG/NACL policy

Then I would inspect CloudTrail and the Terraform diff for the missing or more-specific route

I would add the exact missing prefix through IaC and verify both directions.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route/route_table, TGW or peering resources, TGW propagation/static routes, SG/NACL, provider aliases for cross-account

Resource relationships

The missing remote CIDR must exist end-to-end: source VPC route → interconnect → remote route/propagation → return route → security. One working CIDR proves the link exists, not that every prefix is advertised or permitted.

Production pattern

Represent remote prefixes as reviewed route-intent data and apply them on both sides through the correct account/provider ownership.

Representative Terraform
locals { remote_prefixes = toset(var.remote_service_cidrs) }
resource "aws_route" "to_remote" {
  for_each               = local.remote_prefixes
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.app.id
  destination_cidr_block = each.value
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route" "remote" {
  for_each                       = local.remote_prefixes
  destination_cidr_block         = each.value
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = var.remote_attachment_id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Compare the working and failing prefix at every route domain. Do not add a broad supernet just to make the failing CIDR work; that can create route leaks.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. If connectivity works for some CIDRs but not others, I would treat it as a prefix-specific routing or policy problem rather than an attachment failure.
2. I would trace one working and one failing CIDR through VPC route tables, TGW/peering routes, propagation, return routes and SG/NACL policy.
3. Then I would inspect CloudTrail and the Terraform diff for the missing or more-specific route.
4. I would add the exact missing prefix through IaC and verify both directions.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
When only some CIDRs fail, inspect the exact prefix in VPC/TGW route tables, propagation and security rules rather than the attachment state.

Q26L2HYBRID ROUTING
SCENARIO

On-premises systems can initiate connections into AWS, but AWS workloads cannot initiate connections back on-premises. What would you inspect on both sides?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
On-premises systems can initiate connections into AWS, but AWS workloads cannot initiate connections back on-premises. What would you inspect on both sides
SCOPE
Multi-AZHybrid / On-PremTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deployment
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
AWS Workload → VPC/TGW RT → VPN / DX → On-Prem Router → On-Prem App The failing direction usually points to missing AWS-side routes, on-prem return routes, security policy, or asymmetric path selection.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • On-prem CIDR → TGW/VGW
  • Correct attachment/propagation
  • AWS VPC CIDR learned/installed
  • Firewall allows initiated direction
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Because on-prem can initiate to AWS but AWS cannot initiate back, I would compare the two directions and focus on AWS-side route selection, on-prem return routing and firewalls

I would confirm the AWS subnet/TGW route contains the on-prem prefix, then verify the VPN/DX route is active and the on-prem firewall allows AWS-originated sessions

Flow Logs and on-prem logs help show which side drops the packet

I would correct the missing route or policy and test a new AWS-initiated connection.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpn_connection/TGW or DX resources, VPC routes, TGW routes, on-prem route/BGP config external to AWS Terraform, SG/NACL

Resource relationships

AWS→on-prem initiation needs an AWS-side route to the remote prefix and an on-prem return route to the AWS CIDR. A working on-prem→AWS flow can coexist with a broken reverse initiation if policies/routes differ.

Production pattern

Store the canonical AWS/on-prem prefix sets and BGP/static-routing intent alongside infrastructure code; coordinate on-prem automation separately.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route" "aws_to_onprem" {
  for_each               = toset(var.onprem_cidrs)
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_cidr_block = each.value
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
# TGW route may be propagated from VPN/DX; use a static route only when the design requires it.
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route" "onprem_static" {
  count                          = var.use_static_onprem_routes ? 1 : 0
  destination_cidr_block         = var.onprem_cidrs[0]
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = var.hybrid_attachment_id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Validate effective AWS route, TGW/VGW route, tunnel/BGP advertisement, on-prem return route, firewalls and NAT. Never change tunnel crypto parameters before proving the data-plane routing problem.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. Because on-prem can initiate to AWS but AWS cannot initiate back, I would compare the two directions and focus on AWS-side route selection, on-prem return routing and firewalls.
2. I would confirm the AWS subnet/TGW route contains the on-prem prefix, then verify the VPN/DX route is active and the on-prem firewall allows AWS-originated sessions.
3. Flow Logs and on-prem logs help show which side drops the packet.
4. I would correct the missing route or policy and test a new AWS-initiated connection.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
The failing direction usually points to missing AWS-side routes, on-prem return routes, security policy, or asymmetric path selection.
Q27L2SITE-TO-SITE VPN
SCENARIO

A Site-to-Site VPN has one tunnel down and users report intermittent failures. How do you decide whether the remaining tunnel is sufficient, and what do you check before forcing failover?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A Site-to-Site VPN has one tunnel down and users report intermittent failures. How do you decide whether the remaining tunnel is sufficient, and what do you check before forcing failover
SCOPE
Multi-AZVPNTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deployment
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
AWS VPN gateway ↔ Tunnel 1 ↔ customer gateway AND AWS VPN gateway ↔ Tunnel 2 ↔ customer gateway (parallel redundant tunnels).
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Configure both VPN tunnels on the customer gateway
  • Check tunnel health/BGP or static route state
  • Verify which tunnel AWS and on-prem currently prefer
  • Validate application impact before forcing a path change
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

One VPN tunnel down means redundancy is already degraded even if traffic still passes on the surviving tunnel

I would inspect tunnel telemetry, BGP state or static route status and the customer-gateway logs to determine whether the fault is IKE/IPsec, BGP, or the on-prem device

I would avoid changes that risk the healthy tunnel, restore the failed tunnel separately, and verify traffic can use either path

I would also alert on tunnel state so the environment does not remain silently single-homed.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_customer_gateway, aws_vpn_connection, aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm for TunnelState, routing resources

Resource relationships

One aws_vpn_connection contains two independent tunnels. Both terminate on the same logical AWS VPN connection but have distinct outside IPs and tunnel parameters; routing should continue over the healthy tunnel when designed correctly.

Production pattern

Manage the VPN connection as one resource, consume both tunnel outputs into the customer-gateway configuration, and alarm independently on both tunnel states.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpn_connection" "onprem" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.onprem.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
  static_routes_only  = false
}
locals {
  vpn_tunnels = {
    tunnel1 = aws_vpn_connection.onprem.tunnel1_address
    tunnel2 = aws_vpn_connection.onprem.tunnel2_address
  }
}
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "vpn_tunnel_down" {
  for_each            = local.vpn_tunnels
  alarm_name          = "${each.key}-down"
  namespace           = "AWS/VPN"
  metric_name         = "TunnelState"
  statistic           = "Maximum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 3
  threshold           = 0.5
  comparison_operator = "LessThanThreshold"
  dimensions = {
    VpnId           = aws_vpn_connection.onprem.id
    TunnelIpAddress = each.value
  }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Do not recreate the VPN to troubleshoot one tunnel unless required. Preserve the healthy path, inspect tunnel telemetry/BGP, and test failover during a controlled window.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. One VPN tunnel down means redundancy is already degraded even if traffic still passes on the surviving tunnel.
2. I would inspect tunnel telemetry, BGP state or static route status and the customer-gateway logs to determine whether the fault is IKE/IPsec, BGP, or the on-prem device.
3. I would avoid changes that risk the healthy tunnel, restore the failed tunnel separately, and verify traffic can use either path.
4. I would also alert on tunnel state so the environment does not remain silently single-homed.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
A VPN is designed with two tunnels. Restore redundancy while checking BGP/static routes, tunnel telemetry and customer-gateway configuration.
Q28L2DX FAILOVER
SCENARIO

Direct Connect fails, but traffic does not move to the VPN backup as designed. What routing and BGP evidence would you inspect?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Direct Connect fails, but traffic does not move to the VPN backup as designed. What routing and BGP evidence would you inspect
SCOPE
Multi-AZDirect ConnectVPNTerraform-managedPost-Terraform change
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
AWS VPC/TGW → DX path (primary when healthy) OR VPN path (backup); if DX fails, the VPN route must become usable and the return path must also fail over.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Compare advertised prefixes on DX and VPN
  • Check route propagation/static routes and BGP attributes
  • Verify VPN backup is actually learned/eligible
  • Validate return path and firewall/NAT state
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

If Direct Connect fails and VPN does not take over, I would verify the backup path actually carries the required prefixes before assuming AWS will fail over

I would inspect DX BGP state, VPN tunnel/BGP state, route advertisements on both sides and the effective route preference

I would restore service by making the valid VPN routes active if that is the approved runbook, then fix the routing preference/advertisement issue and perform a controlled failover test.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpn_connection, aws_dx_gateway/association, TGW route tables, CloudWatch alarms; on-prem BGP attributes coordinated externally

Resource relationships

DX and VPN are parallel hybrid paths. Terraform can build both AWS paths, but route preference depends on AWS routing rules plus BGP advertisements/attributes and return-path policy on the customer routers.

Production pattern

Provision and monitor backup VPN before relying on DX. Keep identical required prefixes reachable over both paths and document which attributes/prefix specificity make DX primary.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpn_connection" "backup" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.onprem.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
}
resource "aws_dx_gateway" "primary" {
  name            = "prod-dxgw"
  amazon_side_asn = var.aws_dx_asn
}
# DX gateway/TGW association is owned by the central network stack.
resource "aws_dx_gateway_association" "tgw" {
  dx_gateway_id         = aws_dx_gateway.primary.id
  associated_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  allowed_prefixes      = [for c in var.aws_advertised_cidrs : { prefix = c }]
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Failover testing must validate both forward and return paths. Keep BGP policy in source control on the on-prem side as well; AWS Terraform cannot correct a customer-router advertisement mistake.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. If Direct Connect fails and VPN does not take over, I would verify the backup path actually carries the required prefixes before assuming AWS will fail over.
2. I would inspect DX BGP state, VPN tunnel/BGP state, route advertisements on both sides and the effective route preference.
3. I would restore service by making the valid VPN routes active if that is the approved runbook, then fix the routing preference/advertisement issue and perform a controlled failover test.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Validate that backup prefixes are actually advertised/accepted over VPN and that route preference permits VPN to become active when DX is unavailable.
Q29L2HYBRID DNS
SCENARIO

On-premises clients can resolve AWS private names, but AWS workloads cannot resolve on-premises names. Design the resolver path and identify the likely missing direction.

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
On-premises clients can resolve AWS private names, but AWS workloads cannot resolve on-premises names. Design the resolver path and identify the likely missing direction
SCOPE
Multi-AZHybrid / On-PremTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deployment
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
AWS Workload → Resolver Outbound → VPN / DX → On-Prem DNS → Resolver Inbound AWS-to-on-prem queries need outbound Resolver rules/endpoints; on-prem-to-AWS queries use inbound endpoints. One direction working does not validate the other.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Resolver rules associated with every consuming VPC
  • PHZ associated to required VPCs
  • TGW/VPN/DX routes to endpoint subnets
  • UDP/TCP 53 SG/NACL/firewall allowed
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

The fact that on-prem can resolve AWS names proves the inbound Resolver path works, not the outbound path

For AWS to resolve on-prem names, I would verify an outbound Resolver endpoint, a forwarding rule for the on-prem domain, association of that rule with the VPC, network reachability to the on-prem DNS servers and UDP/TCP 53 rules

I would query from the affected VPC and inspect Resolver query logs

The fix is on the outbound direction, not the inbound endpoint that is already working.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route53_resolver_endpoint inbound/outbound, aws_route53_resolver_rule, association, SG, optional PHZ

Resource relationships

AWS→on-prem DNS uses an OUTBOUND Resolver endpoint plus FORWARD rule association. On-prem→AWS private DNS uses an INBOUND Resolver endpoint and on-prem conditional forwarding to its IPs. They are separate directions and should be shown/configured separately.

Production pattern

Deploy two or more endpoint IPs across AZs, centralize forwarding rules, and use dedicated SG rules for UDP/TCP 53.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_route53_resolver_endpoint" "inbound" {
  name      = "central-in"
  direction = "INBOUND"
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.resolver.id]
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.dns_a.id }
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.dns_b.id }
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_endpoint" "outbound" {
  name      = "central-out"
  direction = "OUTBOUND"
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.resolver.id]
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.dns_a.id }
  ip_address { subnet_id = aws_subnet.dns_b.id }
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule" "onprem" {
  domain_name          = "corp.example.com"
  rule_type            = "FORWARD"
  resolver_endpoint_id = aws_route53_resolver_endpoint.outbound.id
  target_ip { ip = var.onprem_dns_1 }
  target_ip { ip = var.onprem_dns_2 }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Test each direction independently. Verify rule association, on-prem conditional forwarders, UDP/TCP 53 paths and private hosted-zone visibility.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. The fact that on-prem can resolve AWS names proves the inbound Resolver path works, not the outbound path.
2. For AWS to resolve on-prem names, I would verify an outbound Resolver endpoint, a forwarding rule for the on-prem domain, association of that rule with the VPC, network reachability to the on-prem DNS servers and UDP/TCP 53 rules.
3. I would query from the affected VPC and inspect Resolver query logs.
4. The fix is on the outbound direction, not the inbound endpoint that is already working.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
AWS-to-on-prem queries need outbound Resolver rules/endpoints; on-prem-to-AWS queries use inbound endpoints. One direction working does not validate the other.

SCENARIO

Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

If a forwarding rule works in one VPC but not other shared VPCs, I would compare rule associations first

I would verify whether the Resolver rule is shared through RAM where required, accepted by the target account, and associated with each intended VPC

Then I would verify those VPCs can route to the outbound Resolver endpoint and that SG/NACL rules allow DNS
