Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_route53_resolver_rule, aws_ram_resource_share, aws_ram_resource_association, aws_ram_principal_association, aws_route53_resolver_rule_association

Resource relationships

The central networking account owns the Resolver rule; RAM shares the rule ARN with organization/accounts; each consumer VPC must still create a resolver-rule association after the share is accepted/visible.

Production pattern

Automate onboarding so account/VPC creation includes RAM visibility and resolver-rule association, rather than relying on manual acceptance/association.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ram_resource_share" "resolver" {
  name                      = "shared-resolver-rules"
  allow_external_principals = false
}
resource "aws_ram_resource_association" "corp_rule" {
  resource_share_arn = aws_ram_resource_share.resolver.arn
  resource_arn       = aws_route53_resolver_rule.corp.arn
}
resource "aws_ram_principal_association" "org" {
  resource_share_arn = aws_ram_resource_share.resolver.arn
  principal          = var.organizational_unit_arn
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule_association" "consumer" {
  provider         = aws.consumer
  resolver_rule_id = var.shared_rule_id
  vpc_id           = aws_vpc.app.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify share status and consumer association separately. Use Organizations sharing where possible and prevent application teams from creating competing wildcard forwarding rules.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. If a forwarding rule works in one VPC but not other shared VPCs, I would compare rule associations first.
2. I would verify whether the Resolver rule is shared through RAM where required, accepted by the target account, and associated with each intended VPC.
3. Then I would verify those VPCs can route to the outbound Resolver endpoint and that SG/NACL rules allow DNS.
4. I would correct the missing share/association in Terraform and verify resolution from every spoke.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Confirm the Resolver rule is shared and associated with every intended VPC, and that those VPCs can reach the outbound Resolver endpoint.
Q31L2IP EXHAUSTION
SCENARIO

A service scales successfully at the compute layer, but new instances or ENIs fail because the subnet has run out of usable IP addresses. How would you confirm and remediate it?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A service scales successfully at the compute layer, but new instances or ENIs fail because the subnet has run out of usable IP addresses. How would you confirm and remediate it
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Auto Scaling / Pods → Subnet /24 → ENIs → Available IPs Check AvailableIpAddressCount and ENI consumers. The fix is address capacity: larger/additional subnets, better CIDR planning, or workload-specific IP optimization.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • AvailableIpAddressCount by subnet
  • EKS pod density + ENI limits + warm IP targets
  • Add/expand subnets or secondary VPC CIDR
  • Tune CNI prefix delegation/IP targets where appropriate
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would confirm the symptom with AvailableIpAddressCount for the affected subnet and identify the main consumers, such as EC2 ENIs, load balancers or Kubernetes pods

If scaling is blocked because the subnet has no free addresses, adding CPU capacity will not help

Short term I would scale into another suitable subnet/AZ if possible; long term I would add/larger subnets or redesign address allocation with IPAM

I would also add alarms for low free-IP thresholds before autoscaling reaches zero.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_subnet, aws_vpc_ipam_pool_cidr_allocation or CIDR inputs, launch template/ENI consumers, CloudWatch monitoring

Resource relationships

Every ENI consumes subnet address capacity. Scaling can succeed at the ASG/EKS control plane but fail at network-interface creation when free IPs are exhausted.

Production pattern

Size subnets from demand plus failure/headroom, monitor AvailableIpAddressCount, and use IPAM for growth. Expanding or replacing subnet CIDRs is not a trivial in-place fix, so plan secondary CIDRs/new subnets ahead of exhaustion.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_subnet" "app" {
  for_each          = var.app_subnets
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.value.az
  cidr_block        = each.value.cidr
}
check "subnet_capacity" {
  assert {
    condition = alltrue([
      for s in aws_subnet.app : s.available_ip_address_count >= var.min_free_ips
    ])
    error_message = "One or more application subnets are below the minimum free-IP threshold."
  }
}
output "subnet_free_ips" {
  value = {
    for k, s in aws_subnet.app : k => s.available_ip_address_count
  }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Alert before exhaustion and treat subnet expansion as capacity planning, not incident-only remediation. Validate every AZ because one subnet can exhaust while the others remain healthy.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. I would confirm the symptom with AvailableIpAddressCount for the affected subnet and identify the main consumers, such as EC2 ENIs, load balancers or Kubernetes pods.
2. If scaling is blocked because the subnet has no free addresses, adding CPU capacity will not help.
3. Short term I would scale into another suitable subnet/AZ if possible; long term I would add/larger subnets or redesign address allocation with IPAM.
4. I would also add alarms for low free-IP thresholds before autoscaling reaches zero.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Check AvailableIpAddressCount and ENI consumers. The fix is address capacity: larger/additional subnets, better CIDR planning, or workload-specific IP optimization.
Q32L2EKS VPC CNI
SCENARIO

EKS nodes have CPU and memory capacity, but new pods remain Pending because the VPC CNI cannot assign IPs. What AWS networking limits do you inspect?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
EKS nodes have CPU and memory capacity, but new pods remain Pending because the VPC CNI cannot assign IPs. What AWS networking limits do you inspect
SCOPE
Multi-AZEKSTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deployment
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
EKS Pod → aws-node / VPC CNI → Node ENI Limits → Subnet IP Pool Node compute capacity does not guarantee pod-IP capacity. Inspect CNI logs, ENI/IP limits, subnet free addresses and prefix delegation settings.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • AvailableIpAddressCount by subnet
  • EKS pod density + ENI limits + warm IP targets
  • Add/expand subnets or secondary VPC CIDR
  • Tune CNI prefix delegation/IP targets where appropriate
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

EKS nodes having spare CPU does not mean the VPC CNI has addresses available for pods

I would inspect Pending pod events, aws-node logs, subnet free IPs, ENI/IP limits for the node instance type and whether prefix delegation is enabled

If the subnet is exhausted, I would add address capacity or move workloads to additional subnets; if the node ENI limit is the issue, I would adjust node type/CNI settings

Recovery is verified by new pods receiving IPs and becoming Ready.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_eks_addon vpc-cni, aws_subnet, optional secondary VPC CIDR/subnets, node groups/launch templates

Resource relationships

The Amazon VPC CNI assigns VPC IPs to pods (mode/config dependent) through node ENIs. Pod scheduling can therefore be blocked by subnet/ENI/IP limits even when CPU and memory are available.

Production pattern

Manage the vpc-cni add-on version/config explicitly, size pod subnets per AZ, and choose prefix delegation/custom networking only after validating instance/AMI/CNI support and capacity model.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_eks_addon" "vpc_cni" {
  cluster_name                = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  addon_name                  = "vpc-cni"
  addon_version               = var.vpc_cni_version
  resolve_conflicts_on_update = "PRESERVE"
  configuration_values = jsonencode({
    env = { ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION = "true", WARM_PREFIX_TARGET = "1" }
  })
}
resource "aws_subnet" "pods" {
  for_each = var.pod_subnets
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = each.value.cidr
  availability_zone = each.value.az
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Check CNI logs, EC2 ENI limits, free subnet IPs and node instance types before scaling nodes blindly. Roll CNI changes gradually and verify pod-IP allocation per AZ.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. EKS nodes having spare CPU does not mean the VPC CNI has addresses available for pods.
2. I would inspect Pending pod events, aws-node logs, subnet free IPs, ENI/IP limits for the node instance type and whether prefix delegation is enabled.
3. If the subnet is exhausted, I would add address capacity or move workloads to additional subnets; if the node ENI limit is the issue, I would adjust node type/CNI settings.
4. Recovery is verified by new pods receiving IPs and becoming Ready.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Node compute capacity does not guarantee pod-IP capacity. Inspect CNI logs, ENI/IP limits, subnet free addresses and prefix delegation settings.
Q33L2CROSS-AZ COST
SCENARIO

Cross-AZ data-transfer charges spike after a scaling event. How do you find the traffic path that changed and decide whether topology should be adjusted?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Cross-AZ data-transfer charges spike after a scaling event. How do you find the traffic path that changed and decide whether topology should be adjusted
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
App AZ-A → Cross-AZ Hop → NAT / Service AZ-B → Destination Use CUR/Cost Explorer plus Flow Logs to identify high-volume cross-AZ paths; prefer same-AZ NAT and topology-aware service placement when practical.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • CUR/Cost Explorer data-transfer usage types
  • NAT bytes + AZ placement
  • Route private subnet to same-AZ NAT
  • Place interface endpoints per AZ when justified
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would use Cost Explorer/CUR to identify the data-transfer category, then Flow Logs and architecture placement to locate the high-volume cross-AZ path

Common causes are private subnets using a NAT Gateway in another AZ, load-balanced traffic crossing AZs unnecessarily, or shared services placed in a single AZ

I would move egress to same-AZ NAT paths or make service placement topology-aware where appropriate, then verify both cost and availability implications before changing routing.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_subnet, per-AZ aws_nat_gateway, ALB/NLB attributes/targets, route tables; VPC Flow Logs/CloudWatch for evidence

Resource relationships

Cross-AZ charges usually come from topology: workload in AZ-A reaching NAT/endpoint/target in AZ-B or load-balancer behavior that crosses zones. Terraform determines placement and route/target associations.

Production pattern

Keep egress and interface endpoints zonally aligned where practical, use multi-AZ targets, and choose cross-zone load balancing based on resilience vs cost—not by default.

Representative Terraform
locals { az_keys = toset(["a","b","c"]) }
resource "aws_nat_gateway" "az" {
  for_each      = local.az_keys
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public[each.key].id
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat[each.key].id
}
resource "aws_route" "private_default" {
  for_each = local.az_keys
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private[each.key].id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.az[each.key].id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Use Cost Explorer/CUR plus Flow Logs and resource/AZ metadata to prove the expensive path. Optimize only after confirming the availability impact of keeping traffic zonal.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. I would use Cost Explorer/CUR to identify the data-transfer category, then Flow Logs and architecture placement to locate the high-volume cross-AZ path.
2. Common causes are private subnets using a NAT Gateway in another AZ, load-balanced traffic crossing AZs unnecessarily, or shared services placed in a single AZ.
3. I would move egress to same-AZ NAT paths or make service placement topology-aware where appropriate, then verify both cost and availability implications before changing routing.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Use CUR/Cost Explorer plus Flow Logs to identify high-volume cross-AZ paths; prefer same-AZ NAT and topology-aware service placement when practical.
Q34L2FLOW LOGS
SCENARIO

VPC Flow Logs show ACCEPT for a failing connection, but the application still times out. What does ACCEPT actually prove, and where do you go next?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
VPC Flow Logs show ACCEPT for a failing connection, but the application still times out. What does ACCEPT actually prove, and where do you go next
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Client EC2 → SG/NACL → Flow Logs → Server EC2 → App Listener ACCEPT means the VPC controls did not reject the traffic. Next inspect the OS firewall, application listener/bind address, health and dependencies.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • REJECT → AWS network control denied
  • ACCEPT → AWS network accepted packet; app can still fail
  • srcaddr/dstaddr/srcport/dstport/protocol
  • Inspect correct ENI/subnet/time window
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Flow Logs showing ACCEPT means the VPC network controls accepted the traffic; it does not prove the application completed the connection

I would verify the destination IP/port, then check whether the process is listening on that port, its bind address, the OS firewall and application logs

I would also test locally on the destination host

This prevents wasting time changing SGs or routes when AWS has already shown the packet was allowed.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_flow_log plus resources for route/SG/NACL; host/app telemetry outside Terraform

Resource relationships

ACCEPT in Flow Logs means the recorded flow was accepted by the VPC networking controls represented in the log record; it does not prove an application listener responded, that an upstream dependency succeeded, or that all packets in a multi-hop path completed.

Production pattern

Keep Flow Logs enabled as baseline evidence and pair them with service-specific logs/metrics. Terraform should make log coverage part of the VPC module.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_flow_log" "vpc" {
  vpc_id               = aws_vpc.main.id
  traffic_type         = "ALL"
  log_destination_type = "cloud-watch-logs"
  log_destination      = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.flow.arn
  iam_role_arn         = aws_iam_role.flow.arn
  max_aggregation_interval = 60
}
Plan · rollout · verification

If Flow Logs are ACCEPT, move outward to listener/OS firewall/application/target health/return-path evidence instead of repeatedly widening SG/NACL rules.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. Flow Logs showing ACCEPT means the VPC network controls accepted the traffic; it does not prove the application completed the connection.
2. I would verify the destination IP/port, then check whether the process is listening on that port, its bind address, the OS firewall and application logs.
3. I would also test locally on the destination host.
4. This prevents wasting time changing SGs or routes when AWS has already shown the packet was allowed.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
ACCEPT means the VPC controls did not reject the traffic. Next inspect the OS firewall, application listener/bind address, health and dependencies.
Q35L2FLOW LOGS
SCENARIO

VPC Flow Logs show REJECT. How do you determine whether the rejection is caused by a Security Group, NACL, or another path issue?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
VPC Flow Logs show REJECT. How do you determine whether the rejection is caused by a Security Group, NACL, or another path issue
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentProduction
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace the exact source-to-destination path and validate the control plane that owns the behavior.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Source → source SG → subnet NACL → destination SG → server ENI. Use Flow Log 5-tuple plus ENI/subnet context to identify which control rejected the packet.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Flow Log src/dst IP and ports
  • ENI and subnet owning the record
  • SG rules attached to source/destination ENIs
  • NACL ordered inbound/outbound rules and ephemeral return path
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would start with the rejected flow's source/destination IP, ports, protocol, ENI and subnet

Then I would inspect the SGs attached to the ENIs and the NACLs associated with the relevant subnets, including NACL rule order and the return ephemeral ports because NACLs are stateless

I would use CloudTrail if the reject started after a change to see which control was modified

I would change only the confirmed denying rule, then retest and confirm Flow Logs move from REJECT to ACCEPT.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_flow_log, aws_security_group rules, aws_network_acl rules, routes

Resource relationships

A REJECT record narrows the investigation to network controls but still needs tuple/interface/direction context. Compare the rejected source/destination/port with the ENI SG and subnet NACL rules, then verify routing.

Production pattern

Standardize Flow Log fields so incident responders can pivot from interface ID to resource, subnet, SG and route-table ownership.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_flow_log" "vpc" {
  vpc_id               = aws_vpc.main.id
  traffic_type         = "REJECT"
  log_destination_type = "s3"
  log_destination      = aws_s3_bucket.flow.arn
  log_format = join(" ", [
    "$${version}", "$${account-id}", "$${interface-id}", "$${srcaddr}", "$${dstaddr}",
    "$${srcport}", "$${dstport}", "$${protocol}", "$${action}", "$${log-status}"
  ])
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Use the rejected ENI and tuple to identify the exact SG/NACL. Avoid generic “open the SG” changes. Keep NACL rule numbering and SG ownership explicit in code.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks
Scenario-specific troubleshooting order
1. I would start with the rejected flow's source/destination IP, ports, protocol, ENI and subnet.
2. Then I would inspect the SGs attached to the ENIs and the NACLs associated with the relevant subnets, including NACL rule order and the return ephemeral ports because NACLs are stateless.
3. I would use CloudTrail if the reject started after a change to see which control was modified.
4. I would change only the confirmed denying rule, then retest and confirm Flow Logs move from REJECT to ACCEPT.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs
Use the 5-tuple, ENI/subnet context and rule configuration to determine whether the reject is caused by SG policy or a stateless NACL rule/return path.
Q36L2PRIVATE DNS
SCENARIO

A private application is supposed to use an Interface VPC Endpoint for an AWS service, but DNS resolves the service name to public addresses and traffic leaves through NAT. How would you prove and fix the problem?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Interface endpoint exists, but clients resolve/use the public service endpoint.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentPRIVATE DNS
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Check private DNS on the endpoint, VPC DNS settings, resolver behavior, endpoint subnet placement, and endpoint policy/SG.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Workload → Route 53 Resolver → private DNS name → Interface Endpoint ENI → AWS service
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • private_dns_enabled where supported
  • enableDnsSupport / enableDnsHostnames
  • Endpoint ENIs in reachable subnets
  • Endpoint SG allows client traffic
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would compare DNS answers from the affected subnet with the endpoint ENI private IPs. If the service name resolves publicly, I check whether private DNS is enabled for the interface endpoint and whether VPC DNS support is functioning.

Once DNS points to the endpoint ENIs, I verify the endpoint SG, policy, routes to the endpoint ENIs, and application port. I would confirm NAT bytes drop after the fix.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_endpoint Interface, private_dns_enabled, endpoint SG, VPC enable_dns_support/hostnames

Resource relationships

With private DNS enabled, the standard regional service hostname resolves to Interface Endpoint ENI IPs inside the VPC. If it still resolves publicly, verify private DNS, VPC DNS settings and any custom DNS forwarding/PHZ conflicts.

Production pattern

Enable private DNS by default for standard AWS-service Interface Endpoints unless a deliberate custom DNS design requires otherwise.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = var.vpc_cidr
  enable_dns_support   = true
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
}
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "api" {
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name        = var.aws_service_name
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = local.private_subnet_ids
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.vpce.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify DNS before route changes. Use dig to confirm private endpoint IPs and compare NAT bytes after remediation. Check for conflicting private zones/Resolver rules.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Resolve the service FQDN from the affected workload.
  2. Compare answer with endpoint ENI addresses.
  3. Check private DNS and VPC DNS attributes.
  4. Check endpoint SG/policy.
  5. Verify traffic no longer traverses NAT.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

A created endpoint is not enough; name resolution determines whether clients actually use it.

Q37L2BLACKHOLE ROUTE
SCENARIO

A peering connection was removed during cleanup. Hours later, one application loses connectivity and its route table shows a blackhole route. How do you recover safely?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
A stale route still points to a deleted or invalid network target.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentBLACKHOLE ROUTE
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Identify the blackhole route, confirm intended connectivity, restore/replace the target through Terraform, and validate the return path.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Source subnet → route table → BLACKHOLE target ✕ → remote VPC
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Route destination prefix
  • Peering/TGW target state
  • Reverse route
  • Terraform ownership of both connection and route
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would first prove the impacted destination matches the blackhole route, then determine whether the deleted peering connection should be restored or whether the route should point to a replacement architecture.

For immediate recovery I use the last known-good design and make the change through the owning Terraform stack if time allows; if an emergency console fix is required, I reconcile it back into state immediately after service is restored.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_vpc_peering_connection, aws_route, Terraform state/import if out-of-band deletion occurred

Resource relationships

A route referencing a deleted peering connection becomes blackhole. Recovery requires either recreating/accepting the intended peering and updating routes, or removing the obsolete route if the dependency should no longer exist.

Production pattern

Use prevent-destroy/policy approval on critical interconnects where justified and ensure dependency mapping exists before cleanup.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "critical" {
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.app.id
  peer_vpc_id = aws_vpc.shared.id
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}
resource "aws_route" "shared" {
  route_table_id            = aws_route_table.app.id
  destination_cidr_block    = aws_vpc.shared.cidr_block
  vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.critical.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

For a live incident, restore the approved dependency first. Then reconcile Terraform state/code, run a fresh plan, and add dependency/route tests so a cleanup PR cannot silently strand routes.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Confirm destination matches the blackhole prefix.
  2. Check target resource lifecycle/CloudTrail.
  3. Validate remote return route.
  4. Restore the intended target/route.
  5. Reconcile Terraform and add dependency/validation guardrails.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

This tests incident recovery plus IaC ownership rather than only route-table syntax.

Q38L2AZ EGRESS
SCENARIO

A vendor API is reachable from workloads in AZ-A but times out from AZ-B. The same application version and Security Group are used in both AZs. How do you narrow the problem?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Same application and SG; external connectivity fails only from one Availability Zone.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentAZ EGRESS
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Compare AZ-specific subnet association, default route, NAT path/EIP, NACL, DNS answer and vendor allow-listing.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
App-B → Private RT-B → NAT-B/EIP-B → IGW → vendor API
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Private-B associated with RT-B
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT-B
  • NAT-B EIP
  • Vendor permits NAT-B public IP if allow-listed
Corrected / Recommended Architecture full working topology
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Because the failure is AZ-specific, I compare the working AZ-A network path to AZ-B before changing the application. I check the private route-table association, NAT target, NAT public EIP, NACLs and DNS result.

If the vendor allow-lists source IPs, I verify NAT-B's EIP is included. That is a common reason for one-AZ external API failures when the AWS path itself is healthy.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

per-AZ route tables/NATs/endpoints, aws_security_group/NACL, aws_flow_log, DNS resources if vendor hostname is used

Resource relationships

Identical application/SG state across AZs shifts suspicion to zonal infrastructure: subnet route association, NAT/endpoint ENI, NACL or DNS path. Terraform should encode per-AZ parity.

Production pattern

Represent each AZ as the same typed object (subnet, RT, NAT, endpoint placement) and validate parity in CI.

Representative Terraform
locals {
  az = {
    a = { subnet = aws_subnet.private_a.id, rt = aws_route_table.private_a.id, nat = aws_nat_gateway.a.id }
    b = { subnet = aws_subnet.private_b.id, rt = aws_route_table.private_b.id, nat = aws_nat_gateway.b.id }
  }
}
resource "aws_route" "vendor_egress" {
  for_each               = local.az
  route_table_id         = each.value.rt
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = each.value.nat
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Compare AZ-A and AZ-B effective config before making changes. Test from both AZs and inspect NAT metrics/Flow Logs to isolate a zonal path issue.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Compare DNS answers in both AZs.
  2. Compare subnet→route-table associations.
  3. Compare NAT targets and EIPs.
  4. Inspect Flow Logs/NAT metrics.
  5. Confirm vendor-side allow-list and test from AZ-B.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

The strongest clue is the working-vs-failing AZ comparison.

Q39L2TGW SUBNET ROUTING
SCENARIO

A new VPC is attached to Transit Gateway and the attachment is Available. Instances in one subnet can reach shared services, but another subnet in the same VPC cannot. What do you check?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
TGW attachment is healthy, but connectivity differs by source subnet.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTransit GatewayTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changeTGW SUBNET ROUTING
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
The VPC attachment state does not configure every subnet route table; compare the route table associated with each source subnet.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Failing subnet → its VPC RT → TGW → TGW RT → shared-services attachment → return route
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Each source subnet route to remote CIDR → TGW
  • TGW route-table association/propagation
  • Shared-services VPC return route
  • SG/NACL
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Available only proves the TGW attachment control-plane state. I compare the VPC route tables associated with the working and failing subnets. The failing subnet often lacks the remote CIDR route to TGW or is associated with a different route table.

Then I verify the TGW route table and the reverse route from shared services. I would use Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer where appropriate to confirm the hop where traffic stops.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment, VPC route tables/associations, TGW route tables

Resource relationships

Only subnets whose associated route tables contain the TGW route can use the attachment. The TGW attachment subnet list itself does not automatically route every workload subnet.

Production pattern

Separate TGW attachment subnets from workload subnets if desired, but ensure every workload route table that needs remote connectivity points the relevant prefixes to TGW.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "app" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  vpc_id             = aws_vpc.app.id
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.tgw_a.id, aws_subnet.tgw_b.id]
}
resource "aws_route" "workload_to_shared" {
  for_each               = aws_route_table.workload
  route_table_id         = each.value.id
  destination_cidr_block = var.shared_services_cidr
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Verify the failing subnet’s actual route-table association first. Then inspect TGW association/propagation and return routes. “Attachment Available” is not a reachability check.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Compare working and failing subnet route-table associations.
  2. Verify remote prefix → TGW.
  3. Check TGW association/propagation.
  4. Verify return route in shared-services VPC.
  5. Check SG/NACL and validate end-to-end.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It prevents the common mistake of treating attachment availability as end-to-end reachability.

Q40L2VPN ROUTING
SCENARIO

Both VPN tunnels show UP, but an EC2 instance still cannot reach an on-premises subnet. What do you investigate before touching the tunnel configuration?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
VPN control plane is up, but the application data path is broken.
SCOPE
Multi-AZVPNTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changeVPN ROUTING
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Check route propagation/advertisements, VPC/TGW routes, on-prem return route, overlapping CIDRs, SG/NACL and OS policy.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
EC2 → VPC route table → VGW/TGW → either VPN tunnel → customer gateway → on-prem subnet.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Remote CIDR route/propagation in VPC/TGW route tables
  • Both tunnels are parallel and can provide redundancy
  • On-prem route back to the VPC CIDR
  • SG/NACL/firewall policy and overlapping CIDRs
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

A tunnel being UP proves IPsec/BGP session health, not application reachability. I first verify whether the exact on-prem prefix is present in the AWS route path and whether the on-prem router has the return route to the VPC.

I also check for overlapping prefixes, SG/NACL rules, and the destination host firewall. I avoid bouncing healthy tunnels until the routing evidence points there.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_customer_gateway, aws_vpn_connection, VPC/TGW routes, SG/NACL; external on-prem routes/firewall

Resource relationships

Tunnel UP proves IKE/IPsec control plane, not that the application prefix is routed. EC2 needs a route to on-prem through VGW/TGW, AWS must learn/contain the remote prefix, on-prem must return the VPC CIDR, and security must permit the flow.

Production pattern

Use dynamic BGP where appropriate and maintain explicit static route intent only when required. Keep tunnel monitoring separate from reachability SLOs.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_vpn_connection" "onprem" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.onprem.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
  static_routes_only  = false
}
resource "aws_route" "to_onprem" {
  for_each               = toset(var.onprem_cidrs)
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private.id
  destination_cidr_block = each.value
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Before tunnel changes, inspect effective prefixes, BGP/static routes, return path, SG/NACL and on-prem firewall logs. Test a specific IP/port to avoid conflating DNS with VPN routing.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Confirm exact source/destination prefixes.
  2. Inspect AWS route to on-prem.
  3. Inspect learned/advertised BGP prefixes.
  4. Verify on-prem return route.
  5. Check SG/NACL/host firewall and test.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

Real incidents frequently have a healthy tunnel and a broken route.

Q41L2BGP PREFERENCE
SCENARIO

Direct Connect is healthy, but production traffic unexpectedly prefers the VPN path. Latency increases. How would you investigate route preference without causing an outage?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Both hybrid paths are healthy, but traffic chooses the less-preferred path.
SCOPE
Multi-AZDirect ConnectVPNTerraform-managedBGP PREFERENCE
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Inspect BGP advertisements/attributes and AWS routing preference, then compare forward and return paths before changing policy.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
AWS VPC/TGW → Direct Connect primary OR Site-to-Site VPN backup → on-premises. The selected path is determined by route specificity and applicable routing/BGP policy, not link health alone.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Prefix length / route specificity on both paths
  • AWS route priority and Direct Connect BGP community/attributes where applicable
  • On-prem BGP local preference/AS path policy
  • Forward and return-path symmetry for stateful devices
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I would confirm the route actually selected on AWS and on-premises, then compare what prefixes and BGP attributes each path advertises. A healthy DX circuit does not guarantee it is the preferred route.

I change routing policy only after verifying the return path and firewall state because a one-sided preference change can create asymmetric traffic or blackholing.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

DX gateway/association, VPN connection, TGW route tables, monitoring; customer-router BGP policy external

Resource relationships

Both DX and VPN advertise/learn routes. Prefix specificity and BGP attributes/routing policy determine the selected path; return-path choice can differ and create asymmetry.

Production pattern

Encode AWS-side allowed prefixes and attachments in Terraform; keep customer-router BGP policy version-controlled in the network automation system and test preference in staging/maintenance windows.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_dx_gateway_association" "core" {
  dx_gateway_id         = aws_dx_gateway.primary.id
  associated_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  allowed_prefixes      = [for p in var.aws_prefixes : { prefix = p }]
}
resource "aws_vpn_connection" "backup" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.onprem.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Do not “fix” preference by withdrawing routes blindly. Capture BGP tables from both sides, identify why VPN wins, change one policy variable at a time, and verify symmetric recovery.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Confirm selected path with routing evidence.
  2. Compare BGP advertisements/attributes.
  3. Inspect AWS route tables/gateway propagation.
  4. Validate return path.
  5. Make controlled preference change and test failback.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

This is the difference between link health and routing intent.

Q42L2EKS SUBNET
SCENARIO

A new EKS managed node group launches successfully in AZ-A but fails repeatedly in AZ-B. The cluster itself is healthy. What AWS networking differences would you compare?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Node-group success depends on AZ/subnet even though the control plane is healthy.
SCOPE
Multi-AZEKSTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changeEKS SUBNET
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Compare free subnet IPs, routes/NAT or required endpoints, NACLs, DHCP/DNS, and security controls between the AZs.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Node in AZ-B → subnet IP allocation → DNS/endpoints/NAT → EKS/ECR/S3/STS dependencies
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • Available subnet IPs
  • Route table/NAT or private endpoints
  • ECR API + DKR + S3 path when private
  • NACL/DNS settings
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Because only AZ-B fails, I compare subnet-level dependencies rather than the EKS control plane. I check available IP addresses first, then route-table association, NAT or VPC endpoints, NACLs, DNS and the node security group.

If the nodes bootstrap but cannot pull images or reach cluster dependencies, ECR/S3/STS endpoint or egress differences are high-probability causes.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_eks_node_group, aws_subnet, route tables/NAT/endpoints, aws_security_group, aws_eks_addon vpc-cni

Resource relationships

A managed node group uses the specified subnets. If AZ-A launches and AZ-B fails, compare subnet free IPs, route-table association, NAT/endpoints/DNS, NACLs and any AZ-specific security or capacity prerequisites.

Production pattern

Pass an explicit multi-AZ subnet set to node groups and enforce a standardized subnet module. Monitor free IP capacity per node subnet.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "system" {
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  node_group_name = "system"
  node_role_arn   = aws_iam_role.nodes.arn
  subnet_ids      = [aws_subnet.private_a.id, aws_subnet.private_b.id]
  scaling_config {
    desired_size = 4
    min_size     = 2
    max_size     = 10
  }
}
resource "aws_route" "private_default" {
  for_each               = aws_route_table.private
  route_table_id         = each.value.id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.az[each.key].id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Compare the two subnet configurations and node bootstrap dependencies before changing EKS itself. Add subnet-capacity alarms and post-deploy node readiness tests per AZ.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Check node-group/EC2 failure reason.
  2. Compare free IPs across subnets.
  3. Compare routes and endpoints/NAT.
  4. Check DNS/NACL/SG.
  5. Launch/test one node and verify bootstrap dependencies.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It tests whether you can use the AZ boundary to narrow a Kubernetes-looking incident to AWS networking.

Q43L2NAT CONNECTIONS
SCENARIO

Private workloads intermittently fail to connect to a high-volume external API. NAT Gateway is Available, but NAT metrics show connection/port pressure. How would you diagnose and mitigate it?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Intermittent external failures under high connection volume despite an Available NAT Gateway.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedPost-Terraform changePost-deploymentNAT CONNECTIONS
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Check NAT connection/error metrics, destination concentration, connection reuse, per-AZ topology, and whether traffic can bypass NAT through private endpoints.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Private workloads → NAT Gateway SNAT pool → external API. If port allocation is exhausted for the same destination tuple, increase NAT IPv4 capacity/distribute egress and reduce connection churn.
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • CloudWatch ErrorPortAllocation and PacketsDropCount
  • Concurrent connections per destination IP:port:protocol
  • Secondary NAT IPv4/EIP capacity and quotas
  • Connection pooling/keep-alive and per-AZ egress distribution
Corrected / Recommended Architecture working target state
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Available is only a control-plane state. I inspect NAT metrics around the failure window and correlate them with application connection counts and destination IPs. High fan-out to a small destination set can create translation pressure.

I also verify clients reuse connections, distribute egress appropriately, and remove AWS-service traffic from NAT with endpoints. The mitigation depends on whether the pressure is architectural or caused by application connection behavior.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_nat_gateway/EIP, routes, aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm; optional additional NAT/EIPs/egress proxy architecture

Resource relationships

NAT Gateway availability is different from available source ports/connections to a destination. High fan-out to the same external endpoint can exhaust translated ports; zonal NAT placement and connection reuse affect pressure.

Production pattern

Alarm on ErrorPortAllocation and connection metrics. Reduce connection churn/reuse connections, distribute destinations/EIPs where architecture permits, or use vendor PrivateLink/private connectivity when available.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "nat_port_errors" {
  for_each            = aws_nat_gateway.az
  alarm_name          = "${each.key}-nat-port-allocation-errors"
  namespace           = "AWS/NATGateway"
  metric_name         = "ErrorPortAllocation"
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 2
  threshold           = 0
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
  dimensions = { NatGatewayId = each.value.id }
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Confirm NAT metrics and destination concentration before adding capacity. Any architectural mitigation must preserve same-AZ routing and be load-tested against the external API behavior.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Correlate failure time with NAT metrics.
  2. Identify top destinations/flows.
  3. Check client connection reuse.
  4. Validate per-AZ NAT path.
  5. Offload eligible AWS traffic and retest.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It tests data-plane capacity and application-network interaction, not just whether the NAT object exists.

Q44L2ASYMMETRIC ROUTING
SCENARIO

After adding centralized network inspection, some TCP sessions establish but reset intermittently. Different directions of the flow appear to traverse different firewall paths. How do you investigate?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Stateful inspection sees asymmetric forward and return paths.
SCOPE
Multi-AZTerraform-managedProductionASYMMETRIC ROUTING
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Trace both directions, inspect TGW route tables/appliance mode and firewall subnet routing, then restore symmetric paths.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
Spoke VPC → TGW → inspection VPC/firewall → egress; return must traverse the compatible inspection path
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • TGW route-table associations
  • Inspection VPC routes
  • Appliance mode where appropriate
  • Per-AZ firewall/NAT topology
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

Stateful inspection depends on the firewall seeing the relevant connection state. I trace the forward and return paths separately and compare TGW route-table decisions, inspection-subnet routes and AZ/appliance behavior.

I would mitigate by restoring the last known symmetric routing design, then fix the route ownership in Terraform and add path tests before rollout.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_ec2_transit_gateway, TGW route tables, aws_networkfirewall_firewall/policy or GWLB endpoints, inspection subnets/routes

Resource relationships

Stateful inspection requires forward and return traffic to traverse a compatible firewall path. TGW appliance mode and route-table design are often required to preserve symmetric flow through inspection appliances.

Production pattern

Use dedicated inspection VPC/subnets, explicit TGW route tables and appliance mode for the inspection attachment where the architecture requires it. Never rely on default propagation for stateful middleboxes.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "inspection" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.core.id
  vpc_id             = aws_vpc.inspection.id
  subnet_ids         = local.tgw_inspection_subnets
  appliance_mode_support = "enable"
}
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route" "spoke_default_to_inspection" {
  destination_cidr_block         = "0.0.0.0/0"
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.spoke.id
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.inspection.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Build path tests for both directions and multiple AZs. A firewall “healthy” check is insufficient if the return route bypasses the same stateful inspection path.

Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

This is a classic senior networking incident where every component can be individually healthy.

Q45L2RAM / RESOLVER
SCENARIO

A Route 53 Resolver rule is shared through AWS RAM. One application account can use it, but a newly onboarded account cannot resolve the on-premises domain. How would you troubleshoot the onboarding gap?

Scenario Contextsymptom / requirement · scope · primary check
SYMPTOM
Shared Resolver rule works for existing accounts but not a newly onboarded account/VPC.
SCOPE
Multi-AZDNS / Route 53Terraform-managedPost-Terraform changeRAM / RESOLVER
FAILURE DOMAIN / PRIMARY CHECK
Verify RAM share acceptance/organization sharing, VPC rule association, resolver endpoint reachability, and network path to on-prem DNS.
Failed / Current ArchitectureAWS architecture · expected path · key configuration points
EXPECTED / TARGET PATH
App VPC → associated Resolver rule → outbound Resolver endpoint → TGW/VPN/DX → on-prem DNS
KEY CONFIGURATION POINTS
  • RAM share/organization permissions
  • Resolver rule associated with the VPC
  • Outbound endpoint SG
  • Routes to on-prem DNS servers
Corrected Path / Fix Delta only what changes
Interview Answer question-specific spoken answer

I compare the working account with the new account: is the rule actually visible through RAM, and is it associated with the new VPC? Sharing a rule and associating it with a VPC are separate steps.

Then I validate the outbound Resolver endpoint security group and network path to the on-prem DNS servers. I test the exact domain through the VPC resolver rather than assuming the shared resource is active.

Terraform Implementation production resources · relationships · HCL · controls
Production resources

aws_ram_resource_share/resource_association/principal_association, aws_route53_resolver_rule_association, provider alias for consumer account

Resource relationships

The shared Resolver rule must be visible to the new account and then associated with its VPC. Sharing and VPC association are separate lifecycle steps.

Production pattern

Make DNS onboarding part of the account/VPC vending pipeline. The central account owns rules; spoke automation owns/requests associations.

Representative Terraform
resource "aws_ram_principal_association" "dns_ou" {
  resource_share_arn = aws_ram_resource_share.dns.arn
  principal          = var.app_ou_arn
}
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule_association" "corp" {
  provider         = aws.spoke
  name             = "corp-forwarding"
  resolver_rule_id = var.shared_corp_rule_id
  vpc_id           = aws_vpc.spoke.id
}
Plan · rollout · verification

Check RAM sharing scope, organization sharing setting, rule visibility and actual VPC association. Validate DNS with a known on-prem FQDN after onboarding.

Troubleshooting Steps evidence-driven checks

Evidence-driven troubleshooting order

  1. Verify RAM share visibility/acceptance.
  2. Check rule association to new VPC.
  3. Check outbound endpoint SG.
  4. Check TGW/VPN/DX routes to DNS servers.
  5. Query the exact domain from the new VPC.
Why this architecture? availability · security · cost · trade-offs

It tests cross-account platform onboarding and DNS, not only Route 53 syntax.
